24	## What was already present
25	
26	The application already used Supabase, Google Drive, Vercel's deadline cron, GitHub forks/collaborator invitations, a database-backed AI review queue and GitHub Actions review workers. Vitest, Playwright, the lifecycle data factory, dedicated test database, local Supabase CI and `pnpm test:sim` also existed.
27	
28	This work adds capture jobs and a capture Actions worker using those services. It does not introduce a new external queue service or database engine. `package.json`, `pnpm-lock.yaml`, `playwright.config.ts`, `vitest.config.ts` and `.github/workflows/test.yml` are unchanged relative to this branch's starting commit. No PGlite dependency remains. New tests and helpers extend the existing suites, so the test content is expanded, not identical to before.
29	
30	Useful existing history: PR #114 made snapshot failure nonfatal after saving; PR #115 separated platform failures from missing Entire evidence and added blocked-attempt logging. The earlier local UI simulation and CI setup are documented in `docs/TESTING.md`. Do not rebuild them.
31	
32	## Implemented changes
33	
34	### Existing flow, active even without the new mode
35	
36	| Change | Files | Why |
37	| --- | --- | --- |
38	| Paginate pending repository invitations | `lib/github.ts` | Invites after the first 100 must be visible |
39	| Reuse SHA from the ref listing and skip matching destination refs | `lib/entire.ts`, `lib/github.ts` | Avoid redundant reads and writes |
40	| Copy Entire refs only for challenges requiring Entire | `lib/actions/submissions.ts`, `lib/submissions-lock.ts` | Eliminate unused evidence work |
41	| Report failed merge-upstream | `lib/github.ts` | Avoid claiming a stale fork was synchronized |
42	| Stop ingest when the review text budget is full | `lib/code-review/ingest.ts` | Stop downloading files that would be discarded |
43	
44	### Opt-in reliable mode
45	
46	`chapters.reliable_submissions` defaults false. The setting is guarded against changes after event start or repository/submission setup. Legacy chapters keep their previous submission flow plus the efficiency fixes above.
47	
48	1. `lib/actions/submissions.ts` routes enabled chapters through `lib/submission-processing/participant.ts` and the authenticated `receive_submission` RPC. Eligibility, deadline, required-field validation, receipt persistence and job creation are transactional. No GitHub call precedes receipt success.
49	2. Repository state distinguishes verification, snapshot and jury access. A receipt may exist while those remain pending. The form polls status only for enabled chapters. Admins use `/admin/submission-processing` to retry or make a reasoned decision.
50	3. Migration `00071_submission_processing.sql` adds the repository/observation/job tables, API budgets/failure records, private review input cache and guarded RPCs. Only service-role workers can write observations or claim jobs. Participant calls use their authenticated client and RLS, not an admin client.
51	4. The worker has `prepare`, `observe` and `finalize` stages, persistent retry times, 90-second leases and repository revisions. Stale workers cannot publish over newer work. Deadline closure freezes received submissions and changes the chapter to pitching without waiting for GitHub.
52	5. GitHub Actions uses bare Git to fetch full ancestry and atomically push the frozen commit and checkpoint refs. It never checks out or executes participant code. Each Git command has a timeout; permanent refusals require review; transient transfers stop after five attempts.
53	6. Captured reviews read one code archive per SHA, with bounded checkpoint archives, and cache immutable input. Archive downloads enforce size/path limits and do not forward credentials to redirects.
54	7. New capture API calls share pacing by GitHub account identity. Different PATs for the same user share that budget. Diagnostics store sanitized failures and selected rate-limit headers. This is not a limiter around every legacy GitHub call.
55	8. Migration `00072_capture_hardening.sql` preserves fork identity and completed individual jury invitations across branch changes and permits capture reads for the database admin email allowlist even with a stale profile role. Reliable captures allow 2,000 checkpoint refs; the legacy REST cap remains 100.
56	
57	There are 70 migration files through 00072. Both capture migrations have only been applied to test databases in this work. Do not infer production migration state from local test success.
58	
59	### Removed or deliberately not built
60	
61	Optional GitHub jury teams were removed at the user's explicit request. Jurors keep individual read invitations; no organization permission or membership changes are part of the feature. The temporary standalone demonstration was removed; the walkthrough is an appended lifecycle test. No direct archive upload, participant-entered commit SHA or GitHub App was implemented. Do not present any of those as existing behavior.
62	
63	## Infrastructure: exact current behavior and problems
64	
65	`vercel.json` currently adds `/api/cron/submission-processing` every minute alongside the existing minute deadline cron. This is a short polling function, not a continuously running worker. The observation target is five minutes per bound repository, then one minute in the final ten minutes. Entire manifests refresh every ten minutes. Actual times can slip under rate limiting.
66	
67	Both Verify and Submit call repository binding, which creates recurring observation and preparation jobs. **The implementation does not wait for the first saved submission.** That is the mismatch the user asked us to revisit.
68	
69	The route loads credentials even when idle, outside its error handler. After observation it counts every pending/running prepare/finalize job, including delayed retries and live leases, and can dispatch every five minutes. Actions concurrency prevents simultaneous workflow bodies but does not eliminate needless queued runs. The worker script drains jobs for up to 20 minutes and exits; a later cron dispatch resumes remaining work.
70	
71	Recommended next adjustment: reuse the existing cron where practical, return before credential lookup when no eligible work exists, dispatch only due work when no worker is active, and start recurring observation only once a receipt exists. An explicit early Verify can do a one-time verification/preparation. Keep database deadline closure independent of long legacy GitHub loops. A reliable dispatch recovery mechanism is still needed: relying only on the submit request to launch a worker would lose recovery if that dispatch fails.
72	
73	### Credentials were not moved in production
74	
75	The new `captureCredentials()` currently requires `app_settings.github_token` and `app_settings.github_org`, unlike the existing `getSettingValue(key, envFallback)` convention. The capture workflows consequently omit `GH_PAT` and organization variables. This was introduced to align identities across cron and Actions; it unnecessarily requires database storage. Settings are stored as text under admin access controls, not encrypted by application code.
76	
77	No Vercel token was removed or copied into production settings. Restore the existing environment fallback convention, and verify the effective bot account in both runtimes. Dispatch permission can use a different credential from private source access, but both source verification and capture must use the account invited by teams. Never print tokens. The legacy `GH_PAT` owner's identity remains unverified; a secret name does not establish identity.
78	
79	The existing test `capture-review-fixes.test.ts` deliberately asserts database-only credentials. A policy change requires a deliberate test update, not weakening an assertion after failure. The project rule requires asking before correcting a genuinely erroneous failing test/mock.
80	
81	### Database guard is not meaningful in Actions yet
82	
83	`scripts/process-submission-captures.ts` compares `CAPTURE_EXPECTED_DATABASE_URL` with `NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL`. Both are assigned from the same secret in each workflow. A wrong test secret therefore passes. Use an independent environment identity/check before any real Actions rehearsal. The current check must not be described as proof of isolation.
84	
85	## Cutoff and event policy: unresolved
86	
87	The frozen SHA is the last platform-observed commit before the deadline, not necessarily the latest commit at that deadline or the exact commit at receipt time. There is no participant-supplied SHA. A successful last-second receipt can have no observation and require review. An outage or quota pause can leave a much older observation.
88	
89	No newer commit is substituted silently. The implementation allows five minutes of access repair after cutoff; platform failures pause the repair timer, and expiry requires organizer review instead of automatically deleting the receipt. An organizer cannot approve a missing frozen capture through the current approve action.
90	
91	Before release, organizers must explicitly accept the cutoff/repair rule or choose a different policy. Recording a team-supplied SHA with the receipt would identify what the team claims to submit and permit later exact fetching; it does not prove that GitHub access or the objects were available at submission time. Do not silently implement a policy change as a technical cleanup.
92	
93	## Incident evidence and fact-check
94	
95	### What is and is not established about rate limits
96	
97	The original baseline is preserved in `github-ratelimit-handoff.md`. It contains internal data and some conclusions that must not be repeated as established causes. Primary/secondary rate-limit response headers were not retained for the historical failed submissions. Generic verification errors can represent access, configuration, rate limiting or platform failure.
98	
99	The corrected checkpoint totals in that baseline are Munich 1,322 and Zurich 770. The earlier script counted repeated copies of the same matching-ref response as pages; the endpoint is not paginated. Old totals and claims of five copies per fork were wrong. These totals were corrected by the prior investigator, not independently remeasured in this handover. Likewise the estimated 216 requests per Zurich-like team is a model, not a measured cost of every submission.
100	
101	The baseline's median 198 review file requests and wasteful ref-copy loops identify plausible quota pressure. They do not prove why any particular team's submission failed. A second PAT for the same user does not create separate capacity. A GitHub App installation may, but no App was built and it would not remove the receipt's dependence on a successful synchronous API call.
102	
103	### Munich: alpha and Tetrad
104	
105	Production rows identify **Tetrad**, not “Tetrot.” Read-only incident queries found 45 submissions, 43 with fork URLs. The two missing fork URLs are:
106	
107	| Team | Receipt time, UTC on 2026-08-23 | Saved deck bytes | Drive creation time, UTC |
108	| --- | --- | ---: | --- |
109	| alpha | 10:39:51.846097 | 294,491 | 10:39:49.304 |
110	| Tetrad | 10:43:39.926206 | 446,055 | 10:43:37.109 |
111	
112	Neither has a matching normal `submission.created` event by project/challenge in the queried logs. This supports the operator's account of manual recovery; absence of an event alone is not proof. Both challenges currently have Entire and jury-fork invitations disabled. Historical values and failed request details were not retained. **The reason their initial attempts failed is unknown.** Do not label this a proven rate-limit incident.
113	
114	The current Munich deadline was edited after the event, so it cannot establish the original cutoff. PR #115's blocked-attempt logging arrived after Munich. The 44 saved Munich decks are all below the platform body ceiling; the largest is 3,813,570 bytes. That does not rule out failed larger originals that were compressed later.
115	
116	Munich's Oasis row has only its repository field and no saved deck URL, despite the current challenge requiring one. No matching Oasis folder was found under the inspected current submission root; that search does not prove no file ever existed. Three retained `client.error` events on `/matches/munich-2` say “Error in input stream” at 09:59:08.469, 10:10:33.720 and 10:10:35.108 UTC. They cannot be attributed to a team, file size or specific upload request.
117	
118	### Zurich: Oasis and the pitch deck
119	
120	All 20 Zurich submissions have fork URLs now. Oasis has a saved PowerPoint of **16,730,665 bytes (16.73 decimal MB)**. Drive metadata says created 2026-09-13 at **10:15:53.961 UTC**, modified **10:15:55.422**, and the submission row was saved at **10:15:56.397099**. There is no matching normal submission-created event in the queried logs. This is consistent with manual recovery.
121	
122	A file of that size cannot pass through the existing participant upload route on Vercel. The route declares a 20 MiB maximum, but Vercel rejects request bodies over about 4.5 MB before route code runs. `SubmissionForm.handleFileUpload` calls `res.json()` before checking status; a text 413 response produces the generic “Upload failed. Please try again.”
123	
124	A local reproduction used the actual handler extracted from the source, a 16,730,665-byte file and a mocked text/plain HTTP 413. The handler attempted the upload, showed exactly that generic message and stored no URL. No live upload was performed. This is a reproduction of the error-handling defect, not a replay of Oasis's original request.
125	
126	**Assessment:** approximately 90% confidence that the oversized deck explains the reported Oasis upload trouble, because the recovered file is far over the platform ceiling and the current handler reproduces the symptom. We do not have the original failed response and cannot rule out another original file or a simultaneous GitHub verification problem. The manual Drive upload script bypasses Vercel's upload endpoint, explaining how the recovered large deck can exist without proving which recovery method was used.
127	
128	GitHub also reported a Zurich-day incident at 08:43–10:44 UTC: https://www.githubstatus.com/incidents/0rn90wk115q9. That timing does not distinguish rate limiting from outage errors for individual teams. Author-controlled commit timestamps likewise do not prove what was submitted on time.
129	
130	### Evidence location and next upload fix
131	
132	The read-only investigation inspected metadata for 64 saved decks across 65 submissions, not deck contents. Its local raw files are `/private/tmp/ehl-pitch-incident-records.json` and `/private/tmp/ehl-pitch-incident-drive.json`. They contain participant/internal URLs and must not be committed. Temporary files may disappear; the useful sanitized sizes, timestamps and limitations are recorded above. No Drive ACLs were changed.
133	
134	References: `app/api/submissions/upload/route.ts`, `components/submission/submission-form.tsx`, `lib/config/upload-limits.ts`, `lib/upload.ts`, `scripts/manual-submission.ts`, `docs/SECURITY.md` upload section and [Vercel's request-body limit](https://vercel.com/docs/functions/limitations#request-body-size).
135	
136	Recommended narrow fix, **not implemented**: reuse the existing 4 MiB upload-limit pattern on client and server, display the limit before upload, handle 413/non-JSON responses explicitly, and offer an accessible Drive/Slides link path for larger decks if organizers want it. Add safe failure metadata through the existing event reporter. Extend current tests for large-file preflight, non-JSON 413, small-file success and required-deck receipt validation. Do not build another upload service unless that product decision is made.
137	
138	## Test with the existing local suite
139	
140	The current ignored `.env.test` points to local Supabase at `127.0.0.1:54321`, uses fake email and blanks GitHub, Drive, AI, SMTP and Redis credentials. `SUPABASE_TEST_MODE=true`; app port 3001. `NODE_OPTIONS` preloads `e2e/helpers/local-network-guard.cjs`. The guard blocks external global fetch calls but is not a general network firewall. Keep external credentials blank. Do not pull production environment variables for these checks or reset the database just to rerun tests.
141	
142	An earlier reviewer reported rebuilding the local database and losing its old test data. Restoration of that older backup was not verified. This handover pass did not reset or rebuild the database; the suite uses its normal E2E fixture cleanup.
143	
144	```bash
145	pnpm typecheck
146	pnpm test
147	pnpm exec dotenv -e .env.test -- pnpm build
148	pnpm test:e2e:lifecycle --grep-invert '7.5 Entire gate'
149	```
150	
151	The excluded existing `7.5 Entire gate` case deliberately calls real GitHub. Excluding it keeps this run local; it is not evidence that the integration passes. A sandbox can block Turbopack's internal localhost port; rerun the same local build with the required execution permission rather than changing application code.
152	
153	To watch 50 actual form submissions, including receipt and capture status:
154	
155	```bash
156	CAPTURE_TEAMS=50 CAPTURE_INSPECT=true pnpm test:e2e:lifecycle --grep 'Submission walkthrough' --headed
157	```
158	
159	This uses separate participant sessions, the real UI, Supabase RPCs, leases and worker. GitHub responses and Git transfer are simulated by `e2e/helpers/capture-github.ts`; AI reviews and jury invitations are disabled for that fixture. The first Inspector pause shows receipts during a simulated 503 outage; Resume restores the simulated provider and drains jobs. The second pause shows the participant and admin screens. Resume again to clean up. Default regression size is three teams; accepted sizes are 1–150. Only one walkthrough should use the test database at a time.
160	
161	The separate 150-receipt test uses sequential RPC submissions. It is not 150 browser users or simultaneous load. The 50-team UI run passed earlier in this work; the final validation below specifies what was rerun for handover. The current walkthrough does not upload pitch decks and does not force a real shared-budget 429 recovery cycle. Unit tests cover quota responses and budget pauses, including two tokens for one account.
162	
163	### Validation at handover
164	
165	| Check rerun for this handover | Result |
166	| --- | --- |
167	| `pnpm typecheck` | Passed |
168	| `pnpm test` | 1,308 tests passed in 121 files, including the local Git transfer check |
169	| Local optimized build with `.env.test` | Passed after granting Turbopack access to its internal local port |
170	| Local lifecycle suite, excluding the live GitHub case | 68 passed in 4.6 minutes against local Supabase |
171	| `git diff --check` | Passed |
172	| New public material credential/internal-reference scan | No matches in the 66 candidate files |
173	
174	Logs are in `/private/tmp/ehl-handover-{typecheck,unit,build,lifecycle}.log`. The lifecycle run uses the default three-team walkthrough plus the separate 150-receipt test. The earlier 50-team UI pass was not rerun at that size during this documentation pass. Real GitHub transfer, Actions dispatch, pitch-deck upload boundaries and simultaneous 150-team browser traffic are not established by these results.
175	
176	## Prioritized next steps for the expert
177	
178	1. Restore appropriate credential fallback and replace the tautological Actions database guard. Keep production configuration untouched while doing so.
179	2. Fix the demonstrated pitch-deck size/error handling using existing helpers and tests. This failure is independent of GitHub rate limits.
180	3. Simplify idle scheduling and make recurring work depend on received submissions. Extend the existing walkthrough to exhaust the shared request budget, show all receipts saved and verify deferred work resumes. Also test no enabled event/no jobs, future retries and a live worker lease.
181	4. Settle the cutoff and repair rules with organizers. If a participant SHA is chosen, test its validation and immutable persistence; do not pretend an observation is the exact submission-time version.
182	5. After independent review and explicit authorization, rehearse private repository access, fork creation, full Git transfer, heavy Entire refs, existing individual jury access and interrupted-worker recovery in a separate test organization. No such GitHub rehearsal has passed yet.
183	6. Review a clean diff against current `main`, confirm no unrelated account changes or private notes, run all appropriate checks, then prepare a PR only when requested. Migrations/configuration/feature enablement are separate release actions, not implied by this handover.
184	
185	Tooling note for the later deployment work: the Vercel plugin reported CLI 59.1.4 as outdated versus 62.0.0. Upgrade with `pnpm add -g vercel@latest` before using it for release configuration. No CLI upgrade or Vercel command was needed for this local handover.
186	
187	Keep the scope centered on accepting submissions under quota pressure and reducing wasted API requests. No jury-team redesign, new database, new demo server or blanket infrastructure migration is needed to solve that problem.

It does not introduce a new external queue service or database engine. `package.json`, `pnpm-lock.yaml`, `playwright.config.ts`, `vitest.config.ts` and `.github/workflows/test.yml` are unchanged relative to this branch's starting commit. No PGlite dependency remains. New tests and helpers extend the existing suites, so the test content is expanded, not identical to before.

Useful existing history: PR #114 made snapshot failure nonfatal after saving; PR #115 separated platform failures from missing Entire evidence and added blocked-attempt logging. The earlier local UI simulation and CI setup are documented in `docs/TESTING.md`. Do not rebuild them.

## Implemented changes

### Existing flow, active even without the new mode

| Change | Files | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Paginate pending repository invitations | `lib/github.ts` | Invites after the first 100 must be visible |
| Reuse SHA from the ref listing and skip matching destination refs | `lib/entire.ts`, `lib/github.ts` | Avoid redundant reads and writes |
| Copy Entire refs only for challenges requiring Entire | `lib/actions/submissions.ts`, `lib/submissions-lock.ts` | Eliminate unused evidence work |
| Report failed merge-upstream | `lib/github.ts` | Avoid claiming a stale fork was synchronized |
| Stop ingest when the review text budget is full | `lib/code-review/ingest.ts` | Stop downloading files that would be discarded |

### Opt-in reliable mode

`chapters.reliable_submissions` defaults false. The setting is guarded against changes after event start or repository/submission setup. Legacy chapters keep their previous submission flow plus the efficiency fixes above.

1. `lib/actions/submissions.ts` routes enabled chapters through `lib/submission-processing/participant.ts` and the authenticated `receive_submission` RPC. Eligibility, deadline, required-field validation, receipt persistence and job creation are transactional. No GitHub call precedes receipt success.
2. Repository state distinguishes verification, snapshot and jury access. A receipt may exist while those remain pending. The form polls status only for enabled chapters. Admins use `/admin/submission-processing` to retry or make a reasoned decision.
3. Migration `00071_submission_processing.sql` adds the repository/observation/job tables, API budgets/failure records, private review input cache and guarded RPCs. Only service-role workers can write observations or claim jobs. Participant calls use their authenticated client and RLS, not an admin client.
4. The worker has `prepare`, `observe` and `finalize` stages, persistent retry times, 90-second leases and repository revisions. Stale workers cannot publish over newer work. Deadline closure freezes received submissions and changes the chapter to pitching without waiting for GitHub.
5. GitHub Actions uses bare Git to fetch full ancestry and atomically push the frozen commit and checkpoint refs. It never checks out or executes participant code. Each Git command has a timeout; permanent refusals require review; transient transfers stop after five attempts.
6. Captured reviews read one code archive per SHA, with bounded checkpoint archives, and cache immutable input. Archive downloads enforce size/path limits and do not forward credentials to redirects.
7. New capture API calls share pacing by GitHub account identity. Different PATs for the same user share that budget. Diagnostics store sanitized failures and selected rate-limit headers. This is not a limiter around every legacy GitHub call.
8. Migration `00072_capture_hardening.sql` preserves fork identity and completed individual jury invitations across branch changes and permits capture reads for the database admin email allowlist even with a stale profile role. Reliable captures allow 2,000 checkpoint refs; the legacy REST cap remains 100.

There are 70 migration files through 00072. Both capture migrations have only been applied to test databases in this work. Do not infer production migration state from local test success.

### Removed or deliberately not built

Optional GitHub jury teams were removed at the user's explicit request. Jurors keep individual read invitations; no organization permission or membership changes are part of the feature. The temporary standalone demonstration was removed; the walkthrough is an appended lifecycle test. No direct archive upload, participant-entered commit SHA or GitHub App was implemented. Do not present any of those as existing behavior.

## Infrastructure: exact current behavior and problems

`vercel.json` currently adds `/api/cron/submission-processing` every minute alongside the existing minute deadline cron. This is a short polling function, not a continuously running worker. The observation target is five minutes per bound repository, then one minute in the final ten minutes. Entire manifests refresh every ten minutes. Actual times can slip under rate limiting.

Both Verify and Submit call repository binding, which creates recurring observation and preparation jobs. **The implementation does not wait for the first saved submission.** That is the mismatch the user asked us to revisit.

The route loads credentials even when idle, outside its error handler. After observation it counts every pending/running prepare/finalize job, including delayed retries and live leases, and can dispatch every five minutes. Actions concurrency prevents simultaneous workflow bodies but does not eliminate needless queued runs. The worker script drains jobs for up to 20 minutes and exits; a later cron dispatch resumes remaining work.

Recommended next adjustment: reuse the existing cron where practical, return before credential lookup when no eligible work exists, dispatch only due work when no worker is active, and start recurring observation only once a receipt exists. An explicit early Verify can do a one-time verification/preparation. Keep database deadline closure independent of long legacy GitHub loops. A reliable dispatch recovery mechanism is still needed: relying only on the submit request to launch a worker would lose recovery if that dispatch fails.

### Credentials were not moved in production

The new `captureCredentials()` currently requires `app_settings.github_token` and `app_settings.github_org`, unlike the existing `getSettingValue(key, envFallback)` convention. The capture workflows consequently omit `GH_PAT` and organization variables. This was introduced to align identities across cron and Actions; it unnecessarily requires database storage. Settings are stored as text under admin access controls, not encrypted by application code.

No Vercel token was removed or copied into production settings. Restore the existing environment fallback convention, and verify the effective bot account in both runtimes. Dispatch permission can use a different credential from private source access, but both source verification and capture must use the account invited by teams. Never print tokens. The legacy `GH_PAT` owner's identity remains unverified; a secret name does not establish identity.

The existing test `capture-review-fixes.test.ts` deliberately asserts database-only credentials. A policy change requires a deliberate test update, not weakening an assertion after failure. The project rule requires asking before correcting a genuinely erroneous failing test/mock.

### Database guard is not meaningful in Actions yet

`scripts/process-submission-captures.ts` compares `CAPTURE_EXPECTED_DATABASE_URL` with `NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL`. Both are assigned from the same secret in each workflow. A wrong test secret therefore passes. Use an independent environment identity/check before any real Actions rehearsal. The current check must not be described as proof of isolation.

## Cutoff and event policy: unresolved

The frozen SHA is the last platform-observed commit before the deadline, not necessarily the latest commit at that deadline or the exact commit at receipt time. There is no participant-supplied SHA. A successful last-second receipt can have no observation and require review. An outage or quota pause can leave a much older observation.

No newer commit is substituted silently. The implementation allows five minutes of access repair after cutoff; platform failures pause the repair timer, and expiry requires organizer review instead of automatically deleting the receipt. An organizer cannot approve a missing frozen capture through the current approve action.

Before release, organizers must explicitly accept the cutoff/repair rule or choose a different policy. Recording a team-supplied SHA with the receipt would identify what the team claims to submit and permit later exact fetching; it does not prove that GitHub access or the objects were available at submission time. Do not silently implement a policy change as a technical cleanup.

## Incident evidence and fact-check

### What is and is not established about rate limits

The original baseline is preserved in `github-ratelimit-handoff.md`. It contains internal data and some conclusions that must not be repeated as established causes. Primary/secondary rate-limit response headers were not retained for the historical failed submissions. Generic verification errors can represent access, configuration, rate limiting or platform failure.

The corrected checkpoint totals in that baseline are Munich 1,322 and Zurich 770. The earlier script counted repeated copies of the same matching-ref response as pages; the endpoint is not paginated. Old totals and claims of five copies per fork were wrong. These totals were corrected by the prior investigator, not independently remeasured in this handover. Likewise the estimated 216 requests per Zurich-like team is a model, not a measured cost of every submission.

The baseline's median 198 review file requests and wasteful ref-copy loops identify plausible quota pressure. They do not prove why any particular team's submission failed. A second PAT for the same user does not create separate capacity. A GitHub App installation may, but no App was built and it would not remove the receipt's dependence on a successful synchronous API call.

### Munich: alpha and Tetrad

Production rows identify **Tetrad**, not “Tetrot.” Read-only incident queries found 45 submissions, 43 with fork URLs. The two missing fork URLs are:

| Team | Receipt time, UTC on 2026-08-23 | Saved deck bytes | Drive creation time, UTC |
| --- | --- | ---: | --- |
| alpha | 10:39:51.846097 | 294,491 | 10:39:49.304 |
| Tetrad | 10:43:39.926206 | 446,055 | 10:43:37.109 |

Neither has a matching normal `submission.created` event by project/challenge in the queried logs. This supports the operator's account of manual recovery; absence of an event alone is not proof. Both challenges currently have Entire and jury-fork invitations disabled. Historical values and failed request details were not retained. **The reason their initial attempts failed is unknown.** Do not label this a proven rate-limit incident.

The current Munich deadline was edited after the event, so it cannot establish the original cutoff. PR #115's blocked-attempt logging arrived after Munich. The 44 saved Munich decks are all below the platform body ceiling; the largest is 3,813,570 bytes. That does not rule out failed larger originals that were compressed later.

Munich's Oasis row has only its repository field and no saved deck URL, despite the current challenge requiring one. No matching Oasis folder was found under the inspected current submission root; that search does not prove no file ever existed. Three retained `client.error` events on `/matches/munich-2` say “Error in input stream” at 09:59:08.469, 10:10:33.720 and 10:10:35.108 UTC. They cannot be attributed to a team, file size or specific upload request.

### Zurich: Oasis and the pitch deck

All 20 Zurich submissions have fork URLs now. Oasis has a saved PowerPoint of **16,730,665 bytes (16.73 decimal MB)**. Drive metadata says created 2026-09-13 at **10:15:53.961 UTC**, modified **10:15:55.422**, and the submission row was saved at **10:15:56.397099**. There is no matching normal submission-created event in the queried logs. This is consistent with manual recovery.

A file of that size cannot pass through the existing participant upload route on Vercel. The route declares a 20 MiB maximum, but Vercel rejects request bodies over about 4.5 MB before route code runs. `SubmissionForm.handleFileUpload` calls `res.json()` before checking status; a text 413 response produces the generic “Upload failed. Please try again.”

A local reproduction used the actual handler extracted from the source, a 16,730,665-byte file and a mocked text/plain HTTP 413. The handler attempted the upload, showed exactly that generic message and stored no URL. No live upload was performed. This is a reproduction of the error-handling defect, not a replay of Oasis's original request.

**Assessment:** approximately 90% confidence that the oversized deck explains the reported Oasis upload trouble, because the recovered file is far over the platform ceiling and the current handler reproduces the symptom. We do not have the original failed response and cannot rule out another original file or a simultaneous GitHub verification problem. The manual Drive upload script bypasses Vercel's upload endpoint, explaining how the recovered large deck can exist without proving which recovery method was used.

GitHub also reported a Zurich-day incident at 08:43–10:44 UTC: https://www.githubstatus.com/incidents/0rn90wk115q9. That timing does not distinguish rate limiting from outage errors for individual teams. Author-controlled commit timestamps likewise do not prove what was submitted on time.

### Evidence location and next upload fix

The read-only investigation inspected metadata for 64 saved decks across 65 submissions, not deck contents. Its local raw files are `/private/tmp/ehl-pitch-incident-records.json` and `/private/tmp/ehl-pitch-incident-drive.json`. They contain participant/internal URLs and must not be committed. Temporary files may disappear; the useful sanitized sizes, timestamps and limitations are recorded above. No Drive ACLs were changed.

References: `app/api/submissions/upload/route.ts`, `components/submission/submission-form.tsx`, `lib/config/upload-limits.ts`, `lib/upload.ts`, `scripts/manual-submission.ts`, `docs/SECURITY.md` upload section and [Vercel's request-body limit](https://vercel.com/docs/functions/limitations#request-body-size).

Recommended narrow fix, **not implemented**: reuse the existing 4 MiB upload-limit pattern on client and server, display the limit before upload, handle 413/non-JSON responses explicitly, and offer an accessible Drive/Slides link path for larger decks if organizers want it. Add safe failure metadata through the existing event reporter. Extend current tests for large-file preflight, non-JSON 413, small-file success and required-deck receipt validation. Do not build another upload service unless that product decision is made.

## Test with the existing local suite

The current ignored `.env.test` points to local Supabase at `127.0.0.1:54321`, uses fake email and blanks GitHub, Drive, AI, SMTP and Redis credentials. `SUPABASE_TEST_MODE=true`; app port 3001. `NODE_OPTIONS` preloads `e2e/helpers/local-network-guard.cjs`. The guard blocks external global fetch calls but is not a general network firewall. Keep external credentials blank. Do not pull production environment variables for these checks or reset the database just to rerun tests.

An earlier reviewer reported rebuilding the local database and losing its old test data. Restoration of that older backup was not verified. This handover pass did not reset or rebuild the database; the suite uses its normal E2E fixture cleanup.

```bash
pnpm typecheck
pnpm test
pnpm exec dotenv -e .env.test -- pnpm build
pnpm test:e2e:lifecycle --grep-invert '7.5 Entire gate'
```

The excluded existing `7.5 Entire gate` case deliberately calls real GitHub. Excluding it keeps this run local; it is not evidence that the integration passes. A sandbox can block Turbopack's internal localhost port; rerun the same local build with the required execution permission rather than changing application code.

To watch 50 actual form submissions, including receipt and capture status:

```bash
CAPTURE_TEAMS=50 CAPTURE_INSPECT=true pnpm test:e2e:lifecycle --grep 'Submission walkthrough' --headed
```

This uses separate participant sessions, the real UI, Supabase RPCs, leases and worker. GitHub responses and Git transfer are simulated by `e2e/helpers/capture-github.ts`; AI reviews and jury invitations are disabled for that fixture. The first Inspector pause shows receipts during a simulated 503 outage; Resume restores the simulated provider and drains jobs. The second pause shows the participant and admin screens. Resume again to clean up. Default regression size is three teams; accepted sizes are 1–150. Only one walkthrough should use the test database at a time.

The separate 150-receipt test uses sequential RPC submissions. It is not 150 browser users or simultaneous load. The 50-team UI run passed earlier in this work; the final validation below specifies what was rerun for handover. The current walkthrough does not upload pitch decks and does not force a real shared-budget 429 recovery cycle. Unit tests cover quota responses and budget pauses, including two tokens for one account.

### Validation at handover

| Check rerun for this handover | Result |
| --- | --- |
| `pnpm typecheck` | Passed |
| `pnpm test` | 1,308 tests passed in 121 files, including the local Git transfer check |
| Local optimized build with `.env.test` | Passed after granting Turbopack access to its internal local port |
| Local lifecycle suite, excluding the live GitHub case | 68 passed in 4.6 minutes against local Supabase |
| `git diff --check` | Passed |
| New public material credential/internal-reference scan | No matches in the 66 candidate files |

Logs are in `/private/tmp/ehl-handover-{typecheck,unit,build,lifecycle}.log`. The lifecycle run uses the default three-team walkthrough plus the separate 150-receipt test. The earlier 50-team UI pass was not rerun at that size during this documentation pass. Real GitHub transfer, Actions dispatch, pitch-deck upload boundaries and simultaneous 150-team browser traffic are not established by these results.

## Prioritized next steps for the expert

1. Restore appropriate credential fallback and replace the tautological Actions database guard. Keep production configuration untouched while doing so.
2. Fix the demonstrated pitch-deck size/error handling using existing helpers and tests. This failure is independent of GitHub rate limits.
3. Simplify idle scheduling and make recurring work depend on received submissions. Extend the existing walkthrough to exhaust the shared request budget, show all receipts saved and verify deferred work resumes. Also test no enabled event/no jobs, future retries and a live worker lease.
4. Settle the cutoff and repair rules with organizers. If a participant SHA is chosen, test its validation and immutable persistence; do not pretend an observation is the exact submission-time version.
5. After independent review and explicit authorization, rehearse private repository access, fork creation, full Git transfer, heavy Entire refs, existing individual jury access and interrupted-worker recovery in a separate test organization. No such GitHub rehearsal has passed yet.
6. Review a clean diff against current `main`, confirm no unrelated account changes or private notes, run all appropriate checks, then prepare a PR only when requested. Migrations/configuration/feature enablement are separate release actions, not implied by this handover.

Tooling note for the later deployment work: the Vercel plugin reported CLI 59.1.4 as outdated versus 62.0.0. Upgrade with `pnpm add -g vercel@latest` before using it for release configuration. No CLI upgrade or Vercel command was needed for this local handover.

Keep the scope centered on accepting submissions under quota pressure and reducing wasted API requests. No jury-team redesign, new database, new demo server or blanket infrastructure migration is needed to solve that problem.

--- CHANGES.md head:
# Changes

## 2026-09-30: Submission reliability draft and investigation handover

### What changed

1. **Existing GitHub flow:** paginate invitations, reuse listed checkpoint SHAs, skip identical refs, and copy Entire evidence only when required. Failed upstream synchronization is reported. Review ingest stops downloading once its text budget is full.
2. **Opt-in submissions:** persist a receipt and repository jobs atomically before GitHub work. Add database-owned observations, deadline closure, leased capture jobs, shared API pacing and failure diagnostics through migrations 00071 and 00072.
3. **Capture and review:** GitHub Actions copies frozen commits with bare Git; review input comes from bounded commit archives. Participant status and organizer retry/decision screens distinguish received submissions from completed captures. Existing individual jury access remains; optional jury-team support was removed.
4. **Tests:** extend the existing Vitest and Playwright suites, including a local bare Git copy check, 150 sequential database receipts and a configurable UI walkthrough. No dependencies, test runner configuration or standalone demo server were added.
5. **Documentation and cleanup:** update the existing feature, setup, security and testing guides. Consolidate the code map and unresolved requirements in `docs/SUBMISSION_CAPTURE_REVIEW.md`, clarify worker contracts in comments, and ignore private investigation notes and local tooling. The operator handover is deliberately excluded from the public change set.

### Root cause

Synchronous GitHub checks could prevent a database receipt, while redundant checkpoint copying and file-by-file review downloads consumed request capacity. Receipt decoupling and request reduction address those mechanisms. Historical team failures cannot all be attributed to rate limits because the original response details were not retained.

content.text:
I checked everything; the handover is accurate. The branch is **safe to commit and push**, provided the commit is rebuilt on today's `main`. It is **not yet safe to merge**: merging deploys to production, and two things would break there unless done in the right order.

## What I checked

| Check | Result |
|---|---|
| Typecheck, unit tests, build | ✅ pass (**1,308 of 1,308** unit tests) |
| E2E against local Supabase, outside keys blank, network guard on | ✅ **69 of 69** |
| Same changes applied on top of today's `main` (#120, #121) | ✅ typecheck passes, **1,343 of 1,343** unit tests; one trivial test-file conflict |
| Privacy scan of the 66 files that would be committed (public repo) | ✅ no tokens, project IDs, internal emails or team names |
| Private notes (`handover.md`, `github-ratelimit-handoff.md`, `.env.test`, `.auth/`) | ✅ all gitignored; they won't be committed |
| Handover's claims against the code | ✅ accurate, including the issues it lists as open |

## What the branch fixes and adds, in simple terms

**Fixes that apply to every match right away:**
- Copies session-history refs only for challenges that actually require Entire.
- Skips refs the copy already has.
- Stops the AI review from downloading files it throws away.
- Finds the bot's pending invites even when there are more than 100.
- Reports a failed copy update instead of pretending it worked.

**New optional mode (off by default, switched on per match):**
- **Submitting only saves to our database**, so GitHub being slow or down can't block a submission.
- A background job notes each repo's latest version during the event and makes the copy early.
- **At the deadline the database freezes one version per team** and the match moves to "pitching" immediately.
- A GitHub Actions worker then copies exactly that version for the jury.
- New admin page "Submission processing" to see status and retry, plus a status box on the participant form.

## Safe to commit?

**Committing and pushing the branch: yes.**
- A pushed branch doesn't deploy: Vercel only deploys `main` and `staging`.
- The new workflows only run once they're on `main`.

One catch: this branch still contains **3 old commits of the account-application feature** (`1e419b7`, `17639fa`, `bf28432`). `main` already has that feature as a squashed merge (#53) with identical content. So the commit should go on a fresh branch from current `main`, or a PR would show that feature twice. The only conflict is in the E2E spec, where both sides added tests at the end of the file; keeping both resolves it.

**Merging to `main` (which deploys to production): not yet.**

1. **Migrations must reach production first.** If the code deploys before 00071 exists, the existing deadline cron asks for a column that doesn't exist, gets an error it ignores, and silently stops locking matches at the deadline. A manual lock also fails. This affects **every** match, not only ones using the new mode.
2. **The new cron errors every minute until the settings exist.** It loads the GitHub settings even when no match uses the new mode, and production doesn't have them yet.

**Also open before switching the mode on for a match**, most of them listed in the handover:
- A **plain 403 from GitHub still stops a team's capture permanently** and sends it to review. That's the kind of error Zurich produced during GitHub's outage. The handover doesn't mention this one.
- The worker's database safety check compares a value with itself, so it protects nothing.
- Credentials are read only from the database, with no environment fallback.
- **Nothing has run against real GitHub yet.**
- Organizers still need to agree the "last observed version before the deadline" rule.

## What you need to do by hand

**Before merging:**
1. **Apply migrations 00071 and 00072 to production Supabase**, then run `pnpm db:check` to confirm.
2. **Admin → Settings in production**: enter the GitHub token (`ehl-gg`) and the org name `european-hackathon-league`. Alternatively, I change the cron to skip everything when no match uses the new mode.
3. **Vercel**: confirm `GITHUB_REPO` is set, since the cron uses it to start the Actions worker. I didn't read Vercel's settings.

**In GitHub: nothing to create for production.**
- The bot, the org and the Actions secrets already exist.
- The workflows switch on when merged.
- Jury teams were removed, so the org permission change I mentioned earlier is no longer needed for this feature.

**Before using the mode at an event:**
1. Create a **test GitHub account and test org**, put their details in the **test** database's settings, and do one real trial run with private repos, jury access and an interrupted worker.
2. Agree the cutoff rule with organizers.
3. Only then switch the mode on for a match.

**Separate from this branch but urgent for the finale:** pitch-deck uploads between 4.5 MB and 20 MB fail with a vague "Upload failed". The route allows 20 MB, but Vercel rejects anything over 4.5 MB before the code runs, and the form has no size check. Zurich's Oasis deck was 16.7 MB.

Should I build the clean commit on a fresh branch from `main`, with the conflict resolved? After that I can fix the two merge blockers (cron idle check, safe behavior when the migration isn't applied yet) and the 403 handling. Nothing gets pushed without your go-ahead.

# Changes

## 2026-10-01: One submission flow with queued repository copies

### What changed

1. Submit saves through one authenticated database transaction. Eligibility, required fields and the deadline are checked there; the receipt and copy job are saved together. GitHub is never called on this path.
2. The existing deadline cron dispatches only due copy jobs to a small GitHub Actions worker. Saves, resubmissions, final locks and admin retries queue work. There is no second submission mode, extra cron, periodic repository observation or separate processing dashboard.
3. The worker copies the resolved commit and required Entire refs using bare Git, remembers progress, paces REST calls by account and honors rate-limit headers. Crashed or superseded workers cannot publish stale results. Administrators use the existing snapshot status/retry UI. Individual jury invitations remain.
4. Reviews use one bounded archive for the copied SHA. Legacy review downloads stop at their text budget. Invite pagination, listed checkpoint SHA reuse, unchanged-ref skipping and explicit sync failures remain fixed.
5. Removed the unshipped capture-mode schema, participant polling, branch inputs, approval/repair policy, review-input cache and database-only credential requirement. One migration, 00071, adds two job/budget tables and snapshot SHA/error columns. Tokens retain the existing environment/settings convention.
6. Extended the existing Vitest and Playwright suites. Tests for the removed synchronous flow and opt-in mode were deliberately replaced by database-receipt/queue guarantees. Original lifecycle cases, runner configuration, dependencies and CI test workflows are unchanged. Documentation follows the existing feature, setup, security and testing guides.

### Why

Synchronous GitHub verification could reject a submission when the shared account's request quota was exhausted. Redundant checkpoint and review requests added pressure. Saving independently prevents that rejection; bulk copying, bounded ingestion and pacing reduce the quota pressure itself. Historical generic errors alone do not prove every incident was rate limiting.

### Limits

The saved SHA identifies the code actually copied when the job runs. This does not prove the source state at the exact deadline. Real GitHub transfer/permissions and Actions execution still need a test-org rehearsal. The separately investigated pitch-deck upload-size/error-message defect is not changed here.

Everything is local and uncommitted. See [TESTING.md](docs/TESTING.md#submission-queue-tests) for the existing local suite and configurable 50-team walkthrough. The private incident handover is intentionally gitignored.

=================== HANDOVER
# Handover: single submission flow and rate-limit fixes

Local operator note, 2026-10-01. **Do not commit this file.** Incident details are private; this file is gitignored. Public implementation documentation lives in the existing `docs/` guides and `CHANGES.md`.

## Scope and authorization

The user explicitly rejected the second submission mode, recurring repository checks, additional jury-team logic and a standalone testing environment. The current draft replaces those with one normal submission flow: save to the database, then process the repository copy. Do not reintroduce the removed architecture under another name.

Everything remains unstaged and uncommitted on `feat/submission-reliability`, starting at `bf28432`. Nothing was pushed or deployed. The branch inherits three earlier account-application commits (`1e419b7`, `17639fa`, `bf28432`); isolate those from the eventual rate-limit PR to main. No rebase/reset/cherry-pick has been performed. Production access was previously authorized only for incident reads; this simplification made no production requests or changes.

Read `AGENTS.md`, `CLAUDE.md`, `RULES.md` and `docs/TESTING.md`. Keep credentials, raw incident files and this note out of commits. Keep all work local until instructed otherwise.

## What remains

1. `lib/actions/submissions.ts` calls authenticated `receive_submission`. The RPC checks membership, check-in, challenge registration, fields and deadline, then saves the receipt. A trigger queues a copy in the same transaction. No verification, fork, Entire check or workflow dispatch can delay Submit. The existing Verify button provides optional feedback.
2. `00071_submission_snapshots.sql` adds `snapshot_sha`/`snapshot_error`, `submission_snapshot_jobs` and `github_request_budgets`. Worker tables/functions are service-role only. Direct participant table writes are refused. Locking and receipt share the chapter lock. Queue results require a live lease and matching revision, so a crash or resubmission cannot publish stale work.
3. The existing deadline cron locks submissions, advances to pitching, and dispatches due jobs only. No extra cron route or schedule remains. Before a saved job exists, there is no repository polling or GitHub request from this path. A live worker suppresses duplicate dispatch; jobs delayed by quota are dispatched when due.
4. `lib/submission-snapshots/worker.ts` resolves each source's current default-branch SHA when a job runs, creates/reuses its fork, and persists progress. `git-transfer.ts` fetches full ancestry and pushes the commit and required Entire refs in bulk, using bare Git without checkout/hooks. Up to 2,000 checkpoint refs are supported. It verifies the destination commit, retains copied progress on retry, and uses individual jury read invitations at final lock.
5. The Actions runner follows the existing code-review worker pattern. It holds the existing database cron lock, runs at most 20 minutes, and exits when no job is due. Quota errors obey retry/reset headers without consuming the five transient failure attempts. Permanent errors are visible on the existing submission detail page; its retry button requeues work.
6. Snapshot REST calls use one account-based budget table, including pacing, hourly write allowance and remaining-quota headroom. This is not a limiter around every legacy GitHub consumer. Bot identification also treats rate-limit responses as retryable. API failures retain sanitized messages and selected rate headers; Git stderr is not persisted.
7. Completed final copies queue existing code reviews atomically. Review code downloads one archive for the recorded SHA; bounded ZIP parsing limits paths, expansion and files, and avoids credential forwarding to the archive host. Legacy review ingestion stops once its text budget is full.
8. Existing GitHub helper fixes remain: invitation pagination, reuse of listed SHAs, skip unchanged refs and report failed merge-upstream. Matching-ref listings are not paginated. Required Entire refs are copied only on the worker path for challenges requiring them.

## Removed

The chapter `reliable_submissions` flag, extra admin screen/sidebar, participant capture polling, custom branch inputs, recurring observations, repair/approval policy, review-input cache, separate cron endpoint, and database-only credential requirement are gone. The two unshipped capture migrations were replaced by one 00071 migration. No GitHub App, team-based jury access, user SHA field, upload fallback or new package was added.

There are 69 migration files through 00071. The prior draft's data was only local/test state. Do not apply the old draft migrations before this one on a new deployment. The already-running local stack was updated transactionally by removing only its obsolete draft objects and applying the replacement; the whole database was not reset. The previous worktree draft is backed up at `.auth/submission-draft-before-simplification.tar.gz` (ignored), with an expanded copy in `/private/tmp/ehl-draft-before-simplification-20261001/`.

## Infrastructure and credentials

The app retains `GITHUB_TOKEN` and `GITHUB_REPO` for dispatch. Production Actions uses the existing `GH_PAT`, `SUPABASE_URL`, and `SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY` secrets. Configuration uses the existing settings lookup with environment fallback; the token was never removed from Vercel or moved into a production database. No new table stores credentials.

Production organization selection uses the existing app setting, optional `GITHUB_ORG` Actions variable, then existing fallback. Confirm that the effective source token is the account teams invite. The test workflow requires `TEST_GH_PAT` and `TEST_GITHUB_ORG`, uses test database secrets, and refuses missing explicit test credentials/org instead of inheriting deployment defaults. `SNAPSHOT_WORKER_ENV` is set by each workflow and checked against the pre-existing independent production database identity helper.

The workflow files must be on the default branch for repository dispatch. No workflow was run against GitHub in this simplification. Before release: apply the replacement migration, verify secret/account selection and permissions, and run a real private-repository transfer in a separate test org. Local tests do not establish actual GitHub push behavior or Actions startup.

## Timing and remaining limits

This restores the prior practical copy timing: an early copy after save, another after final lock. It does not introduce a new deadline evidence policy. The recorded SHA is resolved when the queued copy starts and reused on retry. If GitHub quota delays that first resolution, later pushes can be copied. Do not claim the exact deadline state was captured. There is no participant-entered SHA or recurring observation system.

A persisted receipt does not prove repository access or Entire evidence. Those checks now run in the worker and surface errors to organizers. File upload remains a separate earlier request and its oversized-pitch-deck defect is still open. The quota fix cannot repair that upload failure.

## Testing and public-repository review

`package.json`, `pnpm-lock.yaml`, Playwright/Vitest configuration, `vercel.json` and the existing CI test workflow are unchanged from the branch base. No PGlite, separate demo application or new dependency remains. The test content is expanded, not identical to before. Tests for the removed synchronous/opt-in behavior were intentionally replaced; original lifecycle cases remain unchanged.

The current `.env.test` targets local Supabase (`127.0.0.1:54321`), blanks external service credentials and preloads the opt-in local fetch guard for child processes. The guard is not a general network firewall. Do not pull production credentials or reset the DB to rerun tests. See `docs/TESTING.md#submission-queue-tests` for the 50-team UI walkthrough and standard commands.

Validation results and any remaining test setup correction are recorded below after the final local run. The existing live-GitHub Entire case is excluded from local-only runs. The 150-receipt test is sequential; it is not a simultaneous load benchmark. A separate local bare-Git unit test verifies full ancestry and ref transfer without real GitHub.

## Incident evidence and fact-check

### What is and is not established about rate limits

The original baseline is preserved in `github-ratelimit-handoff.md`. It contains internal data and some conclusions that must not be repeated as established causes. Primary/secondary rate-limit response headers were not retained for the historical failed submissions. Generic verification errors can represent access, configuration, rate limiting or platform failure.

The corrected checkpoint totals in that baseline are Munich 1,322 and Zurich 770. The earlier script counted repeated copies of the same matching-ref response as pages; the endpoint is not paginated. Old totals and claims of five copies per fork were wrong. These totals were corrected by the prior investigator, not independently remeasured in this handover. Likewise the estimated 216 requests per Zurich-like team is a model, not a measured cost of every submission.

The baseline's median 198 review file requests and wasteful ref-copy loops identify plausible quota pressure. They do not prove why any particular team's submission failed. A second PAT for the same user does not create separate capacity. A GitHub App installation may, but no App was built and it would not remove the receipt's dependence on a successful synchronous API call.

### Munich: alpha and Tetrad

Production rows identify **Tetrad**, not “Tetrot.” Read-only incident queries found 45 submissions, 43 with fork URLs. The two missing fork URLs are:

| Team | Receipt time, UTC on 2026-08-23 | Saved deck bytes | Drive creation time, UTC |
| --- | --- | ---: | --- |
| alpha | 10:39:51.846097 | 294,491 | 10:39:49.304 |
| Tetrad | 10:43:39.926206 | 446,055 | 10:43:37.109 |

Neither has a matching normal `submission.created` event by project/challenge in the queried logs. This supports the operator's account of manual recovery; absence of an event alone is not proof. Both challenges currently have Entire and jury-fork invitations disabled. Historical values and failed request details were not retained. **The reason their initial attempts failed is unknown.** Do not label this a proven rate-limit incident.

The current Munich deadline was edited after the event, so it cannot establish the original cutoff. PR #115's blocked-attempt logging arrived after Munich. The 44 saved Munich decks are all below the platform body ceiling; the largest is 3,813,570 bytes. That does not rule out failed larger originals that were compressed later.

Munich's Oasis row has only its repository field and no saved deck URL, despite the current challenge requiring one. No matching Oasis folder was found under the inspected current submission root; that search does not prove no file ever existed. Three retained `client.error` events on `/matches/munich-2` say “Error in input stream” at 09:59:08.469, 10:10:33.720 and 10:10:35.108 UTC. They cannot be attributed to a team, file size or specific upload request.

### Zurich: Oasis and the pitch deck

All 20 Zurich submissions have fork URLs now. Oasis has a saved PowerPoint of **16,730,665 bytes (16.73 decimal MB)**. Drive metadata says created 2026-09-13 at **10:15:53.961 UTC**, modified **10:15:55.422**, and the submission row was saved at **10:15:56.397099**. There is no matching normal submission-created event in the queried logs. This is consistent with manual recovery.

A file of that size cannot pass through the existing participant upload route on Vercel. The route declares a 20 MiB maximum, but Vercel rejects request bodies over about 4.5 MB before route code runs. `SubmissionForm.handleFileUpload` calls `res.json()` before checking status; a text 413 response produces the generic “Upload failed. Please try again.”

A local reproduction used the actual handler extracted from the source, a 16,730,665-byte file and a mocked text/plain HTTP 413. The handler attempted the upload, showed exactly that generic message and stored no URL. No live upload was performed. This is a reproduction of the error-handling defect, not a replay of Oasis's original request.

**Assessment:** approximately 90% confidence that the oversized deck explains the reported Oasis upload trouble, because the recovered file is far over the platform ceiling and the current handler reproduces the symptom. We do not have the original failed response and cannot rule out another original file or a simultaneous GitHub verification problem. The manual Drive upload script bypasses Vercel's upload endpoint, explaining how the recovered large deck can exist without proving which recovery method was used.

GitHub also reported a Zurich-day incident at 08:43–10:44 UTC: https://www.githubstatus.com/incidents/0rn90wk115q9. That timing does not distinguish rate limiting from outage errors for individual teams. Author-controlled commit timestamps likewise do not prove what was submitted on time.

### Evidence location and next upload fix

The read-only investigation inspected metadata for 64 saved decks across 65 submissions, not deck contents. Its local raw files are `/private/tmp/ehl-pitch-incident-records.json` and `/private/tmp/ehl-pitch-incident-drive.json`. They contain participant/internal URLs and must not be committed. Temporary files may disappear; the useful sanitized sizes, timestamps and limitations are recorded above. No Drive ACLs were changed.

References: `app/api/submissions/upload/route.ts`, `components/submission/submission-form.tsx`, `lib/config/upload-limits.ts`, `lib/upload.ts`, `scripts/manual-submission.ts`, `docs/SECURITY.md` upload section and [Vercel's request-body limit](https://vercel.com/docs/functions/limitations#request-body-size).

Recommended narrow fix, **not implemented**: reuse the existing 4 MiB upload-limit pattern on client and server, display the limit before upload, handle 413/non-JSON responses explicitly, and offer an accessible Drive/Slides link path for larger decks if organizers want it. Add safe failure metadata through the existing event reporter. Extend current tests for large-file preflight, non-JSON 413, small-file success and required-deck receipt validation. Do not build another upload service unless that product decision is made.

`package.json`, `pnpm-lock.yaml`, Playwright/Vitest configuration, `vercel.json` and the existing CI test workflow are unchanged from the branch base. No PGlite, separate demo application or new dependency remains. The test content is expanded, not identical to before. Tests for the removed synchronous/opt-in behavior were intentionally replaced; original lifecycle cases remain unchanged.

The current `.env.test` targets local Supabase (`127.0.0.1:54321`), blanks external service credentials and preloads the opt-in local fetch guard for child processes. The guard is not a general network firewall. Do not pull production credentials or reset the DB to rerun tests. See `docs/TESTING.md#submission-queue-tests` for the 50-team UI walkthrough and standard commands.

Validation results and any remaining test setup correction are recorded below after the final local run. The existing live-GitHub Entire case is excluded from local-only runs. The 150-receipt test is sequential; it is not a simultaneous load benchmark. A separate local bare-Git unit test verifies full ancestry and ref transfer without real GitHub.

## Incident evidence and fact-check

### What is and is not established about rate limits

The original baseline is preserved in `github-ratelimit-handoff.md`. It contains internal data and some conclusions that must not be repeated as established causes. Primary/secondary rate-limit response headers were not retained for the historical failed submissions. Generic verification errors can represent access, configuration, rate limiting or platform failure.

The corrected checkpoint totals in that baseline are Munich 1,322 and Zurich 770. The earlier script counted repeated copies of the same matching-ref response as pages; the endpoint is not paginated. Old totals and claims of five copies per fork were wrong. These totals were corrected by the prior investigator, not independently remeasured in this handover. Likewise the estimated 216 requests per Zurich-like team is a model, not a measured cost of every submission.

The baseline's median 198 review file requests and wasteful ref-copy loops identify plausible quota pressure. They do not prove why any particular team's submission failed. A second PAT for the same user does not create separate capacity. A GitHub App installation may, but no App was built and it would not remove the receipt's dependence on a successful synchronous API call.

### Munich: alpha and Tetrad

Production rows identify **Tetrad**, not “Tetrot.” Read-only incident queries found 45 submissions, 43 with fork URLs. The two missing fork URLs are:

| Team | Receipt time, UTC on 2026-08-23 | Saved deck bytes | Drive creation time, UTC |
| --- | --- | ---: | --- |
| alpha | 10:39:51.846097 | 294,491 | 10:39:49.304 |
| Tetrad | 10:43:39.926206 | 446,055 | 10:43:37.109 |

Neither has a matching normal `submission.created` event by project/challenge in the queried logs. This supports the operator's account of manual recovery; absence of an event alone is not proof. Both challenges currently have Entire and jury-fork invitations disabled. Historical values and failed request details were not retained. **The reason their initial attempts failed is unknown.** Do not label this a proven rate-limit incident.

The current Munich deadline was edited after the event, so it cannot establish the original cutoff. PR #115's blocked-attempt logging arrived after Munich. The 44 saved Munich decks are all below the platform body ceiling; the largest is 3,813,570 bytes. That does not rule out failed larger originals that were compressed later.

Munich's Oasis row has only its repository field and no saved deck URL, despite the current challenge requiring one. No matching Oasis folder was found under the inspected current submission root; that search does not prove no file ever existed. Three retained `client.error` events on `/matches/munich-2` say “Error in input stream” at 09:59:08.469, 10:10:33.720 and 10:10:35.108 UTC. They cannot be attributed to a team, file size or specific upload request.

### Zurich: Oasis and the pitch deck

All 20 Zurich submissions have fork URLs now. Oasis has a saved PowerPoint of **16,730,665 bytes (16.73 decimal MB)**. Drive metadata says created 2026-09-13 at **10:15:53.961 UTC**, modified **10:15:55.422**, and the submission row was saved at **10:15:56.397099**. There is no matching normal submission-created event in the queried logs. This is consistent with manual recovery.

A file of that size cannot pass through the existing participant upload route on Vercel. The route declares a 20 MiB maximum, but Vercel rejects request bodies over about 4.5 MB before route code runs. `SubmissionForm.handleFileUpload` calls `res.json()` before checking status; a text 413 response produces the generic “Upload failed. Please try again.”

A local reproduction used the actual handler extracted from the source, a 16,730,665-byte file and a mocked text/plain HTTP 413. The handler attempted the upload, showed exactly that generic message and stored no URL. No live upload was performed. This is a reproduction of the error-handling defect, not a replay of Oasis's original request.

**Assessment:** approximately 90% confidence that the oversized deck explains the reported Oasis upload trouble, because the recovered file is far over the platform ceiling and the current handler reproduces the symptom. We do not have the original failed response and cannot rule out another original file or a simultaneous GitHub verification problem. The manual Drive upload script bypasses Vercel's upload endpoint, explaining how the recovered large deck can exist without proving which recovery method was used.

GitHub also reported a Zurich-day incident at 08:43–10:44 UTC: https://www.githubstatus.com/incidents/0rn90wk115q9. That timing does not distinguish rate limiting from outage errors for individual teams. Author-controlled commit timestamps likewise do not prove what was submitted on time.

The read-only investigation inspected metadata for 64 saved decks across 65 submissions, not deck contents. Its local raw files are `/private/tmp/ehl-pitch-incident-records.json` and `/private/tmp/ehl-pitch-incident-drive.json`. They contain participant/internal URLs and must not be committed. entries.name: Monitor
entries.description:
Start a background monitor that streams events from a long-running script. Each stdout line is an event — you keep working and notifications arrive in the chat. Events arrive on their own schedule and are not replies from the user, even if one lands while you're waiting for the user to answer a question.

Pick by how many notifications you need:
- **One** ("tell me when the server is ready / the build finishes") → use **Bash with `run_in_background`** and a command that exits when the condition is true, e.g. `until grep -q "Ready in" dev.log; do sleep 0.5; done`. You get a single completion notification when it exits.
- **One per occurrence, until the monitor expires (re-arm to continue)** ("tell me every time an ERROR line appears") → Monitor with an unbounded command (`tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, `while true`).
- **One per occurrence, until a known end** ("emit each CI step result, stop when the run completes") → Monitor with a command that emits lines and then exits.

Your script's stdout is the event stream. Each line becomes a notification. Exit ends the watch.

  # Each matching log line is an event
  tail -f /var/log/app.log | grep --line-buffered "ERROR"

  # Each file change is an event
  inotifywait -m --format '%e %f' /watched/dir

  # Poll GitHub for new PR comments and emit one line per new comment
  last=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
  while true; do
    now=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
    gh api "repos/owner/repo/issues/123/comments?since=$last" --jq '.[] | "\(.user.login): \(.body)"'
    last=$now; sleep 30
  done

  # Node script that emits events as they arrive (e.g. WebSocket listener)
  node watch-for-events.js

  # Per-occurrence with a natural end: emit each CI check as it lands, exit when the run completes
  prev=""
  while true; do
    s=$(gh pr checks 123 --json name,bucket)
    cur=$(jq -r '.[] | select(.bucket!="pending") | "\(.name): \(.bucket)"' <<<"$s" | sort)
    comm -13 <(echo "$prev") <(echo "$cur")
    prev=$cur
    jq -e 'all(.bucket!="pending")' <<<"$s" >/dev/null && break
    sleep 30
  done

**Don't use an unbounded command for a single notification.** `tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, and `while true` never exit on their own, so the monitor stays armed until timeout even after the event has fired. For "tell me when X is ready," use Bash `run_in_background` with an `until` loop instead (one notification, ends in seconds). Note that `tail -f log | grep -m 1 ...` does *not* fix this: if the log goes quiet after the match, `tail` never receives SIGPIPE and the pipeline hangs anyway.

**Script quality:**
- Every pipe stage must flush per line or matches sit in its buffer unseen: `grep` needs `--line-buffered`, `awk` needs `fflush()`. `head` cannot flush at all — `| head -N` delivers nothing until N matches accumulate, then ends the stream.
- In poll loops, handle transient failures (`curl ... || true`) — one failed request shouldn't kill the monitor.
- Poll intervals: 30s+ for remote APIs (rate limits), 0.5-1s for local checks.
- Write a specific `description` — it appears in every notification ("errors in deploy.log" not "watching logs").
- Only stdout is the event stream. Stderr goes to the output file (readable via Read) but does not trigger notifications — for a command you run directly (e.g. `python train.py 2>&1 | grep --line-buffered ...`), merge stderr with `2>&1` so its failures reach your filter. (No effect on `tail -f` of an existing log — that file only contains what its writer redirected.)

**Coverage — silence is not success.** When watching a job or process for an outcome, your filter must match every terminal state, not just the happy path. A monitor that greps only for the success marker stays silent through a crashloop, a hung process, or an unexpected exit — and silence looks identical to "still running." Before arming, ask: *if this process crashed right now, would my filter emit anything?* If not, widen it.

  # Wrong — silent on crash, hang, or any non-success exit
  tail -f run.log | grep --line-buffered "elapsed_steps="

  # Right — one alternation covering progress + the failure signatures you'd act on
  tail -f run.log | grep -E --line-buffered "elapsed_steps=|Traceback|Error|FAILED|assert|Killed|OOM"

For poll loops checking job state, emit on every terminal status (`succeeded|failed|cancelled|timeout`), not just success. If you cannot confidently enumerate the failure signatures, broaden the grep alternation rather than narrow it — some extra noise is better than missing a crashloop.

**Output volume**: Every stdout line is a conversation message, so the filter should be selective — but selective means "the lines you'd act on," not "only good news." Never pipe raw logs; filter to exactly the success and failure signals you care about. Monitors that produce too many events are automatically stopped; restart with a tighter filter if this happens.

Stdout lines within 200ms are batched into a single notification, so multiline output from a single event groups naturally.

The script runs in the same shell environment as Bash. Exit ends the watch (exit code is reported). Every monitor expires after `timeout_ms` (default 5 minutes, at most 30 minutes): it is killed and you get one notice with the event count. Re-arm it if you still need the watch; for a long watch (PR monitoring, log tails) set `timeout_ms` to the maximum and re-arm on each expiry, and widen the filter if an expiry with no events was unexpected. Use TaskStop to cancel early.
**ws source** — open a WebSocket and stream each incoming text frame as an event. No shell, no polling: the server pushes, you get notified.

  Monitor({
    ws: {url: 'wss://events.example.com/stream', protocols: ['v1']},
    description: 'deploy events',
  })

Each text frame becomes one notification (multiline frames stay as one event). Binary frames are reported as `[binary frame, N bytes]` rather than passed through. Socket close ends the watch with the close code surfaced; errors are surfaced before close. Same rate limiting as bash — a firehose will be suppressed and eventually stopped, so subscribe to a filtered feed where one exists.

Prefer this over `command: 'websocat wss://…'` — it avoids the extra process and line-buffering pitfalls. Use bash when you need to transform or filter frames with shell tools before they become events.

description.description: Short human-readable description of what you are monitoring (shown in notifications).

timeout_ms.description: Kill the monitor after this deadline. Default 300000ms. Deadlines above 1800000ms are capped to 1800000ms. You are notified at expiry and can re-arm.

command.description: Shell command or script. Each stdout line is an event; exit ends the watch.

ws.description: WebSocket to open. Each text frame is an event; binary frames are reported as a placeholder line. Socket close ends the watch. Cannot be combined with command.
