content.content:
**Private submission repositories: options and participant invitations**

Written 3 October 2026. Local discussion record for `fix/submission-snapshot-queue`.

Status: retain these options for a later decision. Participant managed jury invitations and GitHub groups have not been approved for implementation. This note changes no application behavior. It is excluded through `.git/info/exclude` and must stay out of commits and public PRs.

**The problem we are solving is the bot's GitHub quota.** Submission checks, repository copies, jury invitations and reviews previously competed for the same account's capacity. The current branch reduces that work and moves copies into the background. The remaining question is how to provide jury access to private code without hundreds of permission writes from that same bot near the deadline.

The event assumptions discussed are 300 participants, approximately 80 teams based on past rosters, and 100 teams as a conservative scenario. There will be three challenges and at most five jurors per challenge. One challenge, or at most two, may need private repositories. Equal participation would make one third or two thirds of repositories private, but that distribution is an assumption.

Jurors can be assigned around the deadline, approximately two hours before or after it. Private repository access should begin only after the submission deadline. The roster of jurors cannot be assumed complete early in the event.

**The main option to remember: participants invite jurors to their original private repository.** The EHL jury page would open that original repository at the commit already accepted by the platform. The bot would stop inviting those jurors to the copied repository. Participants would send the invitations through their own GitHub accounts.

This removes the jury invitation writes from the bot's account. It leaves a small manual task for each participating team and keeps the existing number of repository invitations that each juror must accept. It does not require an EHL GitHub group or membership in the EHL organization.

**A possible event timeline would be:**

1. During the hackathon, a team creates its repository and gives the existing bot access as today. The bot still needs access to verify the repository, check Entire where required, record the accepted commit and copy the code. Inviting jurors does not replace inviting the bot.
2. The team submits through the existing form. Submit checks the source repository and required Entire evidence, records the exact commit and queues the background copy. An Update Submission before the deadline records a new accepted version. Merely pushing code does not update the submission.
3. Organizers assign jurors to challenges in the existing admin workflow and collect their exact GitHub usernames. Participants receive the usernames for their own challenge, either through ordinary event communication or a small addition to the existing form. The communication choice is still open; no new interface has been approved.
4. At the deadline, the platform closes submissions in the database as planned. The accepted commit stays fixed. Sending invitations later must never select a newer commit or reopen submission editing.
5. After the deadline, each private repository owner invites the assigned jurors directly on GitHub. With five jurors, that is five invitations from that owner. If a juror is assigned later, the team sends the additional invitation then. A replacement juror also requires a new invitation, and removal of the former juror is a separate task.
6. Each juror accepts the GitHub repository invitation. EHL's existing magic link login, challenge assignments, dashboard, ranking and feedback remain unchanged. GitHub invitation acceptance is separate from logging into EHL.
7. The jury opens the accepted version through a link shaped like `https://github.com/OWNER/REPO/tree/RECORDED_SHA`. Public repositories use the same accepted version links and need no invitation for reading.
8. The existing background copy and code review can continue. The proposed change concerns human jury access and its link destination. Removing repository copies entirely would be a separate decision with different evidence and availability consequences.

**The deadline guarantee depends on the commit in the link.** Linking to a repository homepage or `main` would show changing code and would violate the accepted version rule. A link containing the recorded commit SHA identifies the accepted code even if the default branch later changes. The SHA must come from the successful server verified submission, never from a newly resolved branch head when the jury opens the page. [GitHub: permanent links](https://docs.github.com/en/repositories/working-with-files/using-files/getting-permanent-links-to-files)

Teams retain control of their own GitHub repositories. This approach cannot prevent them from making later pushes there. It prevents those later pushes from becoming accepted submission code. Jurors must evaluate the linked commit; GitHub still lets them navigate elsewhere in the repository.

**There is a material permission problem with personally owned private repositories.** GitHub gives their collaborators write access. A personal repository owner cannot grant a juror only read access. Repositories owned by an organization can offer a Read role, subject to that organization's policies. Therefore participant invitations cannot universally satisfy a strict requirement that jurors may only read code. This is a decision blocker if that requirement remains absolute. [GitHub: personal repository permissions](https://docs.github.com/en/repositories/managing-your-repositorys-settings-and-features/repository-access-and-collaboration/permission-levels-for-a-personal-account-repository)

**Access becomes an organizer and participant coordination task.** A mistyped username, a pending invitation, a team leaving immediately after the deadline, or a late jury assignment can still prevent judging. The platform must not claim access is verified just because it displays a link. The smallest operational approach is for jurors to open their assigned repositories and report missing access to the organizers. Automated access verification would need a separate proposal, permission checks and an API request budget.

The after deadline access rule also depends on participants following the timing instruction. Sending an invitation early allows the juror to accept early. Hiding an EHL link does not revoke GitHub access or prevent a juror from visiting the source directly. Public repositories are already readable at any time.

**A recorded SHA guarantees identity, not availability.** A team can revoke access or delete the original repository. Retaining the existing copy is useful for review work and evidence, but a GitHub private fork should not be described as a fully independent archive: GitHub can delete private forks when source access is removed. Stronger independent retention would require a separate design and approval. [GitHub: access after removing a collaborator](https://docs.github.com/en/repositories/managing-your-repositorys-settings-and-features/repository-access-and-collaboration/permission-levels-for-a-personal-account-repository#access-after-removing-a-collaborator)

**The capacity gain is concrete.** The following counts are modeled REST writes from our worker. Assume one repository per team, five jurors per challenge, public repositories receive no jury invitations, all copies are created in the same hourly window, and the bot already has source access. Round private repository counts upward.

| Teams | Private share | Private repositories | Current individual jury writes | Copy plus jury writes | Copy writes if participants invite jurors |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 61 | One third | 21 | 105 | 166 | 61 |
| 61 | Two thirds | 41 | 205 | 266 | 61 |
| 80 | One third | 27 | 135 | 215 | 80 |
| 80 | Two thirds | 54 | 270 | 350 | 80 |
| 100 | One third | 34 | 170 | 270 | 100 |
| 100 | Two thirds | 67 | 335 | 435 | 100 |

The formula for the current individual invitation approach is `worker writes = repositories created + private repositories × jurors`. With participant invitations, the jury term becomes zero for our worker. The invitations still happen, distributed across participant owners. This is a change in who performs the work, not a claim that GitHub has unlimited capacity.

The branch's local limiter allows 400 writes per account per fixed hourly window and spaces writes by three seconds. At 80 teams, one third private leaves 185 writes of margin; two thirds private leaves 50. At 100 teams, those margins become 130 below the cap or 35 above it. The 401st write waits if the same window is still active. [Local implementation](supabase/migrations/00071_submission_snapshots.sql)

If the copies were created in an earlier hourly window, only the jury writes remain near the deadline: 135 or 270 for 80 teams, and 170 or 335 for 100 teams. Those invitation counts fit below 400. Creating a copy a few minutes before the deadline does not necessarily put it in an earlier window.

These calculations exclude retries, repeated submissions, other bot activity, workflow dispatches and accepting pending source invitations. They assume one repository field per submission. Verification and archive downloads still use API requests. Git transfer and invitation acceptance time are additional work, so write spacing is not a guarantee of end to end completion time.

**GitHub's limits and our limiter are different things.** A normal authenticated user has a primary REST budget of 5,000 requests per hour. The documented general secondary thresholds include 80 content requests per minute and 500 per hour, but endpoint accounting and some secondary controls are not public. Our 400 write limit is an exact code rule; GitHub's 500 is a planning benchmark, not a guaranteed allowance for exactly 500 collaborator invitations. Primary and secondary limits can apply independently. [GitHub: REST rate limits](https://docs.github.com/en/rest/using-the-rest-api/rate-limits-for-the-rest-api)

GitHub documents 50 repository invitations per repository per 24 hours, with an exception for existing organization members. Five jurors per repository is comfortably below that repository specific limit, although previous invitations to the same repository also matter. Teams inviting through their own accounts do not consume the EHL bot's primary quota or its database pacing allowance. That does not guarantee that GitHub can never apply another anti abuse restriction. [GitHub: collaborator invitations](https://docs.github.com/en/rest/collaborators/collaborators#add-a-repository-collaborator)

**Public repositories reduce permission work only when we stop sending unnecessary invitations.** Anyone can read a public repository. The current worker checks `invite_jury_to_forks` and does not skip an invitation based on actual repository visibility. For a challenge that requires public repositories, the existing invitation setting can be disabled. For a challenge allowing either visibility, the private fraction alone does not make the current worker skip public ones. That distinction must be retained when using the table above. [Worker](lib/submission-snapshots/worker.ts), [GitHub: repository visibility](https://docs.github.com/en/repositories/creating-and-managing-repositories/about-repositories)

**The Supabase evidence is a dated snapshot, not a forecast.** Read only aggregate queries ran on 2 October 2026, at approximately 21:52 UTC. No production data was changed. These counts have not been refreshed for this note.

| Event | Applications | Accepted, excluding checked in | Checked in | Registered teams | Recorded roster entries | Submissions |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Grand Finale | 231 | 217 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| Munich, August | 456 | 158 | 216 | 52 | 202 | 45 |
| Zurich | 194 | 33 | 79 | 20 | 75 | 20 |

The finale's other 14 applications were pending. There were 61 existing teams with at least one active applicant and 59 with at least one accepted applicant. Only 141 of the 231 applicants belonged to an existing team at query time. Those 61 teams are provisional representations in current membership data, not 61 confirmed finale challenge registrations. There were no finale challenges configured yet. The one third or two thirds private split could therefore not be verified in Supabase.

Munich's recorded rosters averaged `202 / 52 = 3.88` people per team. Zurich averaged `75 / 20 = 3.75`. Applying those averages to 300 participants gives approximately 78 to 80 teams after rounding upward. This is an extrapolation, not a probability or a promise of attendance. Applications, accepted people, checked in people, roster entries and submitted projects are different quantities.

Challenge enrollment was unequal in past events. Munich's 45 submissions split 20, 14 and 11, approximately 44%, 31% and 24%. Zurich's 20 split 11 and 9. One private challenge does not automatically mean only one third of teams are private. The historic challenge setting was `repoAccess: any`, and the saved submissions did not contain repository visibility, so Supabase alone could not establish the actual private share.

The current Zurich assignment records contained three jurors for one challenge and six for the other. The finale calculation deliberately uses the user's new maximum of five per challenge. These assignment records are not proof of successful GitHub invitations or exact historical API traffic.

**The other options discussed remain alternatives.** None is approved by this note.

| Option | Effect on capacity | Main tradeoff |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Another PAT for the same bot | No extra primary quota | Tokens share the account's limit |
| Another organization with the same bot | No extra PAT quota | Useful for access isolation, not capacity by itself |
| A second bot account | Separate primary REST budget | More identities, permissions and routing; no guaranteed doubling of secondary write capacity |
| A GitHub App installation | Separate installation primary budget, with scaling rules | Additional setup and permissions; secondary limits still apply |
| One GitHub group per private challenge | Replaces five grants per private repository with one group grant, plus membership work | Jurors must join the organization and accept membership; ordinary membership has visibility implications |
| Participants invite jurors to originals | Removes our bot's jury invitation writes | Manual coordination, source availability, and write access on personal private repositories |
| Copy earlier with the existing worker | Moves repository creation away from the deadline window | Depends on teams submitting early enough; last minute submissions still create work |

A GitHub App installation starts with at least 5,000 primary requests per hour, can scale with installation repositories and organization users, and has different Enterprise rules. A user token issued through an App still shares the user's primary budget. The exact token type matters. A second token alone is not a capacity plan. [GitHub: authentication and rate limits](https://docs.github.com/en/rest/using-the-rest-api/rate-limits-for-the-rest-api)

With groups, the proposed mapping would be automatic from the existing challenge assignment: create or reuse one group per challenge, grant the group access to that challenge's copied repositories after the deadline, and synchronize assigned jurors into it. Late jurors would join the prepared group instead of requiring grants on every repository. This would need implementation; it is not present on this branch.

For 80 teams and one private challenge, the group model would use about 113 writes including all 80 copies: 27 repository grants, one group creation and five memberships. With two private challenges, about 146. For 100 teams and two private challenges, about 179 instead of 435. These are successful call counts assuming five distinct jurors per private challenge, no retries, and one API membership operation per juror. With only one juror per challenge, groups can add setup work instead of saving it.

GitHub groups live inside an organization. Outside collaborators cannot belong to them. Base permissions would need to be No permission and member privileges reviewed before inviting jurors, otherwise unrelated private code can become visible. Ordinary members can still see organization membership information; a secret group does not turn organization membership into a code only sandbox. Automatic invitations of new organization members also require suitable bot or App permissions. The existing token's sufficiency must be verified rather than assumed. [GitHub: teams](https://docs.github.com/en/organizations/organizing-members-into-teams/about-teams), [base permissions](https://docs.github.com/en/organizations/managing-user-access-to-your-organizations-repositories/managing-repository-roles/setting-base-permissions-for-an-organization), [team membership API](https://docs.github.com/en/rest/teams/members#add-or-update-team-membership-for-a-user)

A separate snapshot organization would isolate these jurors from the main organization's membership and resources. It would still need owners, bot access and permission setup. GitHub Free organizations support private repositories and groups, but cannot receive private forks. Keeping the current private fork method would need an eligible paid plan; creating independent repositories and pushing the accepted objects would require code changes. Paid organization membership can also change seat costs. [GitHub: plans](https://docs.github.com/en/get-started/learning-about-github/githubs-plans), [fork restrictions](https://docs.github.com/en/pull-requests/reference/forks), [license users](https://docs.github.com/en/billing/reference/github-license-users)

Moving the copy to Vercel would not increase the GitHub token's quota. The current Actions worker already performs a bare Git fetch and push of accepted objects without checking out or executing participant code. An independent destination would still have to be created before pushing. Moving execution hosts would require checking Git availability, temporary storage and duration, and adapting the current worker lifetime. There is no measured reason from this discussion to replace the existing worker. If independent copies are ever introduced, disable Actions in their destination before pushing participant workflow files. [GitHub: duplicating repositories](https://docs.github.com/en/repositories/creating-and-managing-repositories/duplicating-a-repository), [organization Actions controls](https://docs.github.com/en/organizations/managing-organization-settings/disabling-or-limiting-github-actions-for-your-organization), [Vercel duration](https://vercel.com/docs/functions/configuring-functions/duration)

The earlier rough effort estimates were 15 to 30 minutes for basic organization creation and permissions, half a day to one day for a tested destination switch, and one to three days for independent copy changes. These were planning estimates with approximately 70% confidence, not measured delivery times. Permission issues and realistic private repository testing can extend them.

**If participant invitations are approved later, keep the implementation narrow.** Reuse the existing challenge assignments, GitHub usernames, source repository URL and accepted SHA. Keep Entire as a blocking Submit check, the service verified receipt, the database deadline lock, the queue, the bot identity and the current review pipeline.

The code already knows the original URL and accepted SHA in `repoSnapshots`. `selectSubmissionRepository` currently prefers the successful fork for the primary repository and falls back to the accepted original commit when a copy is unavailable. It serves both repository links and review inputs. A jury link change must therefore be scoped carefully so that reviews can keep using the copy. Blindly changing this shared selector could alter more behavior than intended. [Selection helper](lib/submission-snapshots/selection.ts), [submission preparation](lib/submission-snapshots/prepare.ts)

Disable automated fork invitations for the affected challenges using the existing setting. Do not add a second submission mode, a new worker, a new secret or a separate testing environment. Whether any additional UI is needed should be decided separately. The smallest first step could be operational instructions plus the narrowly scoped jury link change.

Before implementation, decide whether personal repository write access is acceptable, how juror usernames reach teams, who follows up when a team leaves, and how long access problems may remain unresolved after the deadline. Any grace period must cover access only; it must never allow changing the accepted code. Do not make successful submission depend on a juror accepting an invitation, since jurors may be assigned after the deadline.

Use the existing test suite for any eventual implementation. Cover the original repository link containing the accepted SHA, later pushes leaving that link unchanged, Entire continuing to block invalid submissions, deadline rejection, review inputs staying on the recorded copy, no automatic collaborator PUTs when invitations are disabled, and late or missing jury access being communicated honestly. Real GitHub invitation acceptance and personal versus organization permissions need a rehearsal with test accounts. Existing local mocks cannot prove those external behaviors. Follow the repository's test discipline and approval rules before changing existing assertions.

**The present decision is to keep this as an option.** Participant invitations address the central invitation quota directly. Their strongest counterargument is the permission and coordination burden. GitHub groups reduce repeated invitations while adding organization setup and membership. For approximately 80 teams with one third private, the modeled existing flow already has substantial margin; a larger structural change is not justified by that arithmetic alone.

The earlier interactive calculation is also local at [.auth/github-limit-study/github-invitation-limits.html](.auth/github-limit-study/github-invitation-limits.html). It models all repositories as requiring access grants; use the mixed visibility tables in this note for the one third and two thirds scenarios.

This note records discussion and dated research. It does not certify the branch as ready for release. No application code, production settings or production data were changed while writing it, and no commit or push was made.

**Private submission repositories: options and participant invitations**

Written 3 October 2026. Local discussion record for `fix/submission-snapshot-queue`.

Status: retain these options for a later decision. Participant managed jury invitations and GitHub groups have not been approved for implementation. This note changes no application behavior. It is excluded through `.git/info/exclude` and must stay out of commits and public PRs.

**The problem we are solving is the bot's GitHub quota.** Submission checks, repository copies, jury invitations and reviews previously competed for the same account's capacity. The current branch reduces that work and moves copies into the background. The remaining question is how to provide jury access to private code without hundreds of permission writes from that same bot near the deadline.

The event assumptions discussed are 300 participants, approximately 80 teams based on past rosters, and 100 teams as a conservative scenario. There will be three challenges and at most five jurors per challenge. One challenge, or at most two, may need private repositories. Equal participation would make one third or two thirds of repositories private, but that distribution is an assumption.

Jurors can be assigned around the deadline, approximately two hours before or after it. Private repository access should begin only after the submission deadline. The roster of jurors cannot be assumed complete early in the event.

**The main option to remember: participants invite jurors to their original private repository.** The EHL jury page would open that original repository at the commit already accepted by the platform. The bot would stop inviting those jurors to the copied repository. Participants would send the invitations through their own GitHub accounts.

This removes the jury invitation writes from the bot's account. It leaves a small manual task for each participating team and keeps the existing number of repository invitations that each juror must accept. It does not require an EHL GitHub group or membership in the EHL organization.

**A possible event timeline would be:**

1. During the hackathon, a team creates its repository and gives the existing bot access as today. The bot still needs access to verify the repository, check Entire where required, record the accepted commit and copy the code. Inviting jurors does not replace inviting the bot.
2. The team submits through the existing form. Submit checks the source repository and required Entire evidence, records the exact commit and queues the background copy. An Update Submission before the deadline records a new accepted version. Merely pushing code does not update the submission.
3. Organizers assign jurors to challenges in the existing admin workflow and collect their exact GitHub usernames. Participants receive the usernames for their own challenge, either through ordinary event communication or a small addition to the existing form. The communication choice is still open; no new interface has been approved.
4. At the deadline, the platform closes submissions in the database as planned. The accepted commit stays fixed. Sending invitations later must never select a newer commit or reopen submission editing.
5. After the deadline, each private repository owner invites the assigned jurors directly on GitHub. With five jurors, that is five invitations from that owner. If a juror is assigned later, the team sends the additional invitation then. A replacement juror also requires a new invitation, and removal of the former juror is a separate task.
6. Each juror accepts the GitHub repository invitation. EHL's existing magic link login, challenge assignments, dashboard, ranking and feedback remain unchanged. GitHub invitation acceptance is separate from logging into EHL.
7. The jury opens the accepted version through a link shaped like `https://github.com/OWNER/REPO/tree/RECORDED_SHA`. Public repositories use the same accepted version links and need no invitation for reading.
8. The existing background copy and code review can continue. The proposed change concerns human jury access and its link destination. Removing repository copies entirely would be a separate decision with different evidence and availability consequences.

**The deadline guarantee depends on the commit in the link.** Linking to a repository homepage or `main` would show changing code and would violate the accepted version rule. A link containing the recorded commit SHA identifies the accepted code even if the default branch later changes. The SHA must come from the successful server verified submission, never from a newly resolved branch head when the jury opens the page. [GitHub: permanent links](https://docs.github.com/en/repositories/working-with-files/using-files/getting-permanent-links-to-files)

Teams retain control of their own GitHub repositories. This approach cannot prevent them from making later pushes there. It prevents those later pushes from becoming accepted submission code. Jurors must evaluate the linked commit; GitHub still lets them navigate elsewhere in the repository.

**There is a material permission problem with personally owned private repositories.** GitHub gives their collaborators write access. A personal repository owner cannot grant a juror only read access. Repositories owned by an organization can offer a Read role, subject to that organization's policies. Therefore participant invitations cannot universally satisfy a strict requirement that jurors may only read code. This is a decision blocker if that requirement remains absolute. [GitHub: personal repository permissions](https://docs.github.com/en/repositories/managing-your-repositorys-settings-and-features/repository-access-and-collaboration/permission-levels-for-a-personal-account-repository)

**Access becomes an organizer and participant coordination task.** A mistyped username, a pending invitation, a team leaving immediately after the deadline, or a late jury assignment can still prevent judging. The platform must not claim access is verified just because it displays a link. The smallest operational approach is for jurors to open their assigned repositories and report missing access to the organizers. Automated access verification would need a separate proposal, permission checks and an API request budget.

The after deadline access rule also depends on participants following the timing instruction. Sending an invitation early allows the juror to accept early. Hiding an EHL link does not revoke GitHub access or prevent a juror from visiting the source directly. Public repositories are already readable at any time.

**A recorded SHA guarantees identity, not availability.** A team can revoke access or delete the original repository. Retaining the existing copy is useful for review work and evidence, but a GitHub private fork should not be described as a fully independent archive: GitHub can delete private forks when source access is removed. Stronger independent retention would require a separate design and approval. [GitHub: access after removing a collaborator](https://docs.github.com/en/repositories/managing-your-repositorys-settings-and-features/repository-access-and-collaboration/permission-levels-for-a-personal-account-repository#access-after-removing-a-collaborator)

**The capacity gain is concrete.** The following counts are modeled REST writes from our worker. Assume one repository per team, five jurors per challenge, public repositories receive no jury invitations, all copies are created in the same hourly window, and the bot already has source access. Round private repository counts upward.

| Teams | Private share | Private repositories | Current individual jury writes | Copy plus jury writes | Copy writes if participants invite jurors |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 61 | One third | 21 | 105 | 166 | 61 |
| 61 | Two thirds | 41 | 205 | 266 | 61 |
| 80 | One third | 27 | 135 | 215 | 80 |
| 80 | Two thirds | 54 | 270 | 350 | 80 |
| 100 | One third | 34 | 170 | 270 | 100 |
| 100 | Two thirds | 67 | 335 | 435 | 100 |

The formula for the current individual invitation approach is `worker writes = repositories created + private repositories × jurors`. With participant invitations, the jury term becomes zero for our worker. The invitations still happen, distributed across participant owners. This is a change in who performs the work, not a claim that GitHub has unlimited capacity.

The branch's local limiter allows 400 writes per account per fixed hourly window and spaces writes by three seconds. At 80 teams, one third private leaves 185 writes of margin; two thirds private leaves 50. At 100 teams, those margins become 130 below the cap or 35 above it. The 401st write waits if the same window is still active. [Local implementation](supabase/migrations/00071_submission_snapshots.sql)

If the copies were created in an earlier hourly window, only the jury writes remain near the deadline: 135 or 270 for 80 teams, and 170 or 335 for 100 teams. Those invitation counts fit below 400. Creating a copy a few minutes before the deadline does not necessarily put it in an earlier window.

These calculations exclude retries, repeated submissions, other bot activity, workflow dispatches and accepting pending source invitations. They assume one repository field per submission. Verification and archive downloads still use API requests. Git transfer and invitation acceptance time are additional work, so write spacing is not a guarantee of end to end completion time.

**GitHub's limits and our limiter are different things.** A normal authenticated user has a primary REST budget of 5,000 requests per hour. The documented general secondary thresholds include 80 content requests per minute and 500 per hour, but endpoint accounting and some secondary controls are not public. Our 400 write limit is an exact code rule; GitHub's 500 is a planning benchmark, not a guaranteed allowance for exactly 500 collaborator invitations. Primary and secondary limits can apply independently. [GitHub: REST rate limits](https://docs.github.com/en/rest/using-the-rest-api/rate-limits-for-the-rest-api)

GitHub documents 50 repository invitations per repository per 24 hours, with an exception for existing organization members. Five jurors per repository is comfortably below that repository specific limit, although previous invitations to the same repository also matter. Teams inviting through their own accounts do not consume the EHL bot's primary quota or its database pacing allowance. That does not guarantee that GitHub can never apply another anti abuse restriction. [GitHub: collaborator invitations](https://docs.github.com/en/rest/collaborators/collaborators#add-a-repository-collaborator)

**Public repositories reduce permission work only when we stop sending unnecessary invitations.** Anyone can read a public repository. The current worker checks `invite_jury_to_forks` and does not skip an invitation based on actual repository visibility. For a challenge that requires public repositories, the existing invitation setting can be disabled. For a challenge allowing either visibility, the private fraction alone does not make the current worker skip public ones. That distinction must be retained when using the table above. [Worker](lib/submission-snapshots/worker.ts), [GitHub: repository visibility](https://docs.github.com/en/repositories/creating-and-managing-repositories/about-repositories)

**The Supabase evidence is a dated snapshot, not a forecast.** Read only aggregate queries ran on 2 October 2026, at approximately 21:52 UTC. No production data was changed. These counts have not been refreshed for this note.

| Event | Applications | Accepted, excluding checked in | Checked in | Registered teams | Recorded roster entries | Submissions |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Grand Finale | 231 | 217 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| Munich, August | 456 | 158 | 216 | 52 | 202 | 45 |
| Zurich | 194 | 33 | 79 | 20 | 75 | 20 |

The finale's other 14 applications were pending. There were 61 existing teams with at least one active applicant and 59 with at least one accepted applicant. Only 141 of the 231 applicants belonged to an existing team at query time. Those 61 teams are provisional representations in current membership data, not 61 confirmed finale challenge registrations. There were no finale challenges configured yet. The one third or two thirds private split could therefore not be verified in Supabase.

Munich's recorded rosters averaged `202 / 52 = 3.88` people per team. Zurich averaged `75 / 20 = 3.75`. Applying those averages to 300 participants gives approximately 78 to 80 teams after rounding upward. This is an extrapolation, not a probability or a promise of attendance. Applications, accepted people, checked in people, roster entries and submitted projects are different quantities.

Challenge enrollment was unequal in past events. Munich's 45 submissions split 20, 14 and 11, approximately 44%, 31% and 24%. Zurich's 20 split 11 and 9. One private challenge does not automatically mean only one third of teams are private. The historic challenge setting was `repoAccess: any`, and the saved submissions did not contain repository visibility, so Supabase alone could not establish the actual private share.

The current Zurich assignment records contained three jurors for one challenge and six for the other. The finale calculation deliberately uses the user's new maximum of five per challenge. These assignment records are not proof of successful GitHub invitations or exact historical API traffic.

**The other options discussed remain alternatives.** None is approved by this note.

| Option | Effect on capacity | Main tradeoff |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Another PAT for the same bot | No extra primary quota | Tokens share the account's limit |
| Another organization with the same bot | No extra PAT quota | Useful for access isolation, not capacity by itself |
| A second bot account | Separate primary REST budget | More identities, permissions and routing; no guaranteed doubling of secondary write capacity |
| A GitHub App installation | Separate installation primary budget, with scaling rules | Additional setup and permissions; secondary limits still apply |
| One GitHub group per private challenge | Replaces five grants per private repository with one group grant, plus membership work | Jurors must join the organization and accept membership; ordinary membership has visibility implications |
| Participants invite jurors to originals | Removes our bot's jury invitation writes | Manual coordination, source availability, and write access on personal private repositories |
| Copy earlier with the existing worker | Moves repository creation away from the deadline window | Depends on teams submitting early enough; last minute submissions still create work |

A GitHub App installation starts with at least 5,000 primary requests per hour, can scale with installation repositories and organization users, and has different Enterprise rules. A user token issued through an App still shares the user's primary budget. The exact token type matters. A second token alone is not a capacity plan. [GitHub: authentication and rate limits](https://docs.github.com/en/rest/using-the-rest-api/rate-limits-for-the-rest-api)

With groups, the proposed mapping would be automatic from the existing challenge assignment: create or reuse one group per challenge, grant the group access to that challenge's copied repositories after the deadline, and synchronize assigned jurors into it. Late jurors would join the prepared group instead of requiring grants on every repository. This would need implementation; it is not present on this branch.

For 80 teams and one private challenge, the group model would use about 113 writes including all 80 copies: 27 repository grants, one group creation and five memberships. With two private challenges, about 146. For 100 teams and two private challenges, about 179 instead of 435. These are successful call counts assuming five distinct jurors per private challenge, no retries, and one API membership operation per juror. With only one juror per challenge, groups can add setup work instead of saving it.

GitHub groups live inside an organization. Outside collaborators cannot belong to them. Base permissions would need to be No permission and member privileges reviewed before inviting jurors, otherwise unrelated private code can become visible. Ordinary members can still see organization membership information; a secret group does not turn organization membership into a code only sandbox. Automatic invitations of new organization members also require suitable bot or App permissions. The existing token's sufficiency must be verified rather than assumed. [GitHub: teams](https://docs.github.com/en/organizations/organizing-members-into-teams/about-teams), [base permissions](https://docs.github.com/en/organizations/managing-user-access-to-your-organizations-repositories/managing-repository-roles/setting-base-permissions-for-an-organization), [team membership API](https://docs.github.com/en/rest/teams/members#add-or-update-team-membership-for-a-user)

A separate snapshot organization would isolate these jurors from the main organization's membership and resources. It would still need owners, bot access and permission setup. GitHub Free organizations support private repositories and groups, but cannot receive private forks. Keeping the current private fork method would need an eligible paid plan; creating independent repositories and pushing the accepted objects would require code changes. Paid organization membership can also change seat costs. [GitHub: plans](https://docs.github.com/en/get-started/learning-about-github/githubs-plans), [fork restrictions](https://docs.github.com/en/pull-requests/reference/forks), [license users](https://docs.github.com/en/billing/reference/github-license-users)

Moving the copy to Vercel would not increase the GitHub token's quota. The current Actions worker already performs a bare Git fetch and push of accepted objects without checking out or executing participant code. An independent destination would still have to be created before pushing. Moving execution hosts would require checking Git availability, temporary storage and duration, and adapting the current worker lifetime. There is no measured reason from this discussion to replace the existing worker. If independent copies are ever introduced, disable Actions in their destination before pushing participant workflow files. [GitHub: duplicating repositories](https://docs.github.com/en/repositories/creating-and-managing-repositories/duplicating-a-repository), [organization Actions controls](https://docs.github.com/en/organizations/managing-organization-settings/disabling-or-limiting-github-actions-for-your-organization), [Vercel duration](https://vercel.com/docs/functions/configuring-functions/duration)

The earlier rough effort estimates were 15 to 30 minutes for basic organization creation and permissions, half a day to one day for a tested destination switch, and one to three days for independent copy changes. These were planning estimates with approximately 70% confidence, not measured delivery times. Permission issues and realistic private repository testing can extend them.

**If participant invitations are approved later, keep the implementation narrow.** Reuse the existing challenge assignments, GitHub usernames, source repository URL and accepted SHA. Keep Entire as a blocking Submit check, the service verified receipt, the database deadline lock, the queue, the bot identity and the current review pipeline.

The code already knows the original URL and accepted SHA in `repoSnapshots`. `selectSubmissionRepository` currently prefers the successful fork for the primary repository and falls back to the accepted original commit when a copy is unavailable. It serves both repository links and review inputs. A jury link change must therefore be scoped carefully so that reviews can keep using the copy. Blindly changing this shared selector could alter more behavior than intended. [Selection helper](lib/submission-snapshots/selection.ts), [submission preparation](lib/submission-snapshots/prepare.ts)

Disable automated fork invitations for the affected challenges using the existing setting. Do not add a second submission mode, a new worker, a new secret or a separate testing environment. Whether any additional UI is needed should be decided separately. The smallest first step could be operational instructions plus the narrowly scoped jury link change.

Before implementation, decide whether personal repository write access is acceptable, how juror usernames reach teams, who follows up when a team leaves, and how long access problems may remain unresolved after the deadline. Any grace period must cover access only; it must never allow changing the accepted code. Do not make successful submission depend on a juror accepting an invitation, since jurors may be assigned after the deadline.

Use the existing test suite for any eventual implementation. Cover the original repository link containing the accepted SHA, later pushes leaving that link unchanged, Entire continuing to block invalid submissions, deadline rejection, review inputs staying on the recorded copy, no automatic collaborator PUTs when invitations are disabled, and late or missing jury access being communicated honestly. Real GitHub invitation acceptance and personal versus organization permissions need a rehearsal with test accounts. Existing local mocks cannot prove those external behaviors. Follow the repository's test discipline and approval rules before changing existing assertions.

**The present decision is to keep this as an option.** Participant invitations address the central invitation quota directly. Their strongest counterargument is the permission and coordination burden. GitHub groups reduce repeated invitations while adding organization setup and membership. For approximately 80 teams with one third private, the modeled existing flow already has substantial margin; a larger structural change is not justified by that arithmetic alone.

The earlier interactive calculation is also local at [.auth/github-limit-study/github-invitation-limits.html](.auth/github-limit-study/github-invitation-limits.html). It models all repositories as requiring access grants; use the mixed visibility tables in this note for the one third and two thirds scenarios.

This note records discussion and dated research. It does not certify the branch as ready for release. No application code, production settings or production data were changed while writing it, and no commit or push was made.

Every GitHub-heavy step of a submission ran on the bot's single 5,000/hour REST quota, and most of it ran at the deadline. Since #114 Submit saves first, but the same request then forked the repository and copied up to 100 Entire refs one REST call at a time. The deadline cron re-synced, re-copied and invited jurors for every team inside one function limited to 300 s; at Zurich it never reached `pitching` and an admin had to switch the chapter by hand. Reviews fetched every file separately (replaying the review against the 19 readable Zurich repositories takes 4,569 requests). The jury saw whatever was on the default branch when the lock ran, not a version the team had submitted. Follow-up to #114 and #115.

- **Submit records a verified version, then stops.** It reads the repository and its default-branch head (2 requests; Entire challenges also list and inspect checkpoints) and blocks with a clear message when the bot cannot read the repository, visibility does not match, Entire evidence is missing, or GitHub is unavailable. No fork, ref copy or invite happens in the request.
- **The exact commit is saved.** The service-only `receive_submission` RPC saves the verified commit and checkpoint refs, repeats membership, check-in, registration and deadline checks under the chapter lock, and queues the copy in the same transaction. A later push changes nothing until the team clicks Update Submission; the form says so. Jury links and reviews use the recorded commit.
- **The deadline closes in the database.** `lock_submission_receipts` locks the rows and the chapter moves to `pitching` without calling GitHub. Completed copies and recorded versions are kept.
- **Copies run in a background worker.** The existing minute cron dispatches a GitHub Actions worker only when copy jobs are due. It pushes the recorded commit and Entire refs to the fork with one bare-Git push (no checkout, no hooks), invites jurors at final lock when `invite_jury_to_forks` is on, and remembers progress. Leases and revision checks stop a crashed or superseded run from publishing stale results.
- **Quota is paced instead of exhausted.** Worker REST calls are paced per GitHub account (at most 400 writes per hour, 3 s apart) and honor `retry-after` and `x-ratelimit-reset`; a quota pause does not count as a failure. Worker failure messages and rate-limit headers are logged (never Git stderr). Failures show on the existing admin submission page, whose retry button requeues the job.
- **Reviews download one archive per commit.** One zipball for the recorded commit instead of one request per file. The legacy path stops downloading once its text budget is full instead of fetching and discarding the rest.
- **Shared helpers stop repeating work.** Listed checkpoint SHAs are reused, refs the fork already has are skipped, a pending bot invitation past the first 100 is found, and a failed `merge-upstream` is reported instead of treated as synced.

Submit calls the two service-only RPCs with the admin client after `auth.getUser()`, as `main` already wrote submissions with the admin client; `CLAUDE.md` and `RULES.md` document that single exception. GitHub being unavailable still blocks Submit (as the required Verify did) with a retry message, and a bare 401/403 fails a background copy until an admin retries it.

content.content:
Planned for private repositories (not part of this PR): teams invite their challenge's jurors to their own private repository after the deadline, alongside the bot they already invite, and the jury link opens that repository at the recorded commit (`/tree/<sha>`), so later pushes do not change what is judged. `invite_jury_to_forks` stays off, which takes every jury invitation off the bot's write budget; the worker only creates copies. With five jurors per challenge and 80 teams, that is 135 fewer bot writes when a third of the repositories are private (215 down to 80) and 270 fewer when two thirds are (350 down to 80). At 100 teams with two thirds private it is 335 fewer (435 down to 100), where the bot would otherwise exceed the worker's 400 writes per hour.

120 new unit tests and 10 new lifecycle cases. Typecheck, 1417 unit tests (each commit also passes on its own), build, lifecycle E2E 76/76 on a local Supabase with external calls blocked (the live-GitHub 7.5 case excluded locally) green.

content.text:
Leaving aside the five small fixes, there's one real gap before you squash and merge: **nobody has tested the copy against real GitHub yet**. Everything else is either already checked or a short manual step. Below is the full list in order, with what I verified today (all read-only; I changed nothing).

## ✅ Already in place

| Item | Status |
|---|---|
| CI on PR #122 | **Lint + Types + Unit ✅, E2E Lifecycle ✅** (cross-browser smoke is skipped on PRs, as usual) |
| Production database | **Clean**: 00071/00072 missing (expected), no draft leftovers |
| Production `app_settings` | **No `github_token` / `github_org` override**, so Vercel's `GITHUB_TOKEN` and Actions' `GH_PAT` are used |
| Vercel production variables | `GITHUB_TOKEN`, `GITHUB_ORG`, `GITHUB_REPO`, `CRON_SECRET` all present (the worker is started through `GITHUB_REPO`) |
| Bot `ehl-gg` | admin of `european-hackathon-league`, token scopes `repo` + `workflow` (needed to push repos that contain workflow files), no expiry; may trigger workflows in `tum-ai/ehl` |
| Actions secrets for production | `GH_PAT`, `SUPABASE_URL`, `SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY` exist; you confirmed `GH_PAT` is `ehl-gg` |

## 1. Prepare the test setup (manual, about 30 minutes)

1. **Clean up the test database.** It still holds the old draft: 2 triggers, 14 functions, 6 tables (all empty) and 3 columns. The final 00071 would **fail** there on "already exists". The cleanup script is ready in **`.auth/test-db-remove-draft-capture.sql`** (gitignored). Run it in the **test** project's SQL editor.
2. **Apply 00071, then 00072, to the test database**, also in its SQL editor. **Don't use `scripts/db-migrate.sh`**: it writes to production too. Then run `pnpm db:check:test` to confirm.
3. **Create a test GitHub account and a test org**, with a classic token that has the `repo` + `workflow` scopes. Never use `ehl-gg` or `european-hackathon-league` for testing.

## 2. Real trial run (the actual blocker)

Run the local app against the test database, with the test bot and test org in `.env.test` and `SNAPSHOT_WORKER_ENV=test`. The network guard has to be off for this run only. Then start the worker:

```
pnpm exec dotenv -e .env.test -- pnpm tsx scripts/process-submission-snapshots.ts
```

Check, in this order:
- [ ] private repo **without** the test bot invited → Submit is refused with the "cannot read" message
- [ ] with the bot invited → Submit saves; the recorded commit equals the repo's current commit
- [ ] Entire challenge without evidence → refused; with evidence → saved
- [ ] the worker creates the copy in the test org, and its `ehl-final/…` ref points exactly at the recorded commit
- [ ] a later push alone changes nothing; "Update Submission" records the new commit
- [ ] after the deadline: the chapter is "pitching", and Update is refused
- [ ] the jury link opens the recorded commit (with your manual jury access)
- [ ] stop the worker halfway → the next run continues without breaking anything

Afterwards, put the network guard and the blank keys in `.env.test` back.

## 3. Decide and announce (not code)

- **Tell teams:** pushing after submitting only counts if they click **"Update Submission"** before the deadline.
- **Finale challenges:** leave `invite_jury_to_forks` **off**. Jury access to private repos goes manually, or through teams inviting jurors as in `submission-private-workaround.md`.
- **Repo visibility per challenge** (public, private, or either).

## 4. Merge day, in this order

The finale is still in `applications_open`, so you have a safe window until submissions open on 10 October.

1. Make sure **no match is accepting submissions** right then.
2. **Back up the production database** (Supabase dashboard).
3. Apply **00071, then 00072, to production**, then run `pnpm db:check` to confirm.
4. **Squash & merge #122**, then wait until the Vercel deploy is ready.
5. Check: the admin submissions page loads, and the minute cron runs in the Vercel logs without errors.
6. Optionally run the **"Process submission snapshots-test"** workflow. It needs `TEST_GH_PAT` + `TEST_GITHUB_ORG`, which don't exist in Actions yet, and it can only run after the merge, once the workflow is on `main`.

**If something goes wrong after the merge:** reverting the merge commit is enough. The migrations can stay, because the old code saves with the admin key and passes the new guard. Without the migrations, though, the new code can't run, which is why step 3 comes before step 4.

## Separate from #122, but before the finale

- **Pitch decks between 4.5 and 20 MB** still fail with "Upload failed". This is unchanged by #122.

Should I start with step 1? That means running the cleanup and applying the migrations on the **test** database; I'd do that only after your explicit OK.

The live site responds normally. `/apply` returning 404 is expected: applying happens on each match's own page, not on a general `/apply`.

## Done: 1.1 and 1.2 on test and production

- **Test:** the old draft is removed, the final 00071 and 00072 are applied, and `db:check:test` shows all 66 migrations applied.
- **Production:** 00071 and 00072 are applied in one transaction, and `db:check` shows all 66 applied.
- **Nothing visible changed.** Applications, submissions and copy links are identical before and after, and no match is open for submissions. The code running today keeps working: it saves with the admin key, which the new guard allows.

Things to keep in mind:
- **Until #122 is merged**, production has the new database objects but the old code. That's harmless as long as no match opens for submissions. Merge before the finale opens submissions.
- The test cleanup needed two retries, because of the order in which draft objects depend on each other. Each failed attempt was rolled back completely, so nothing was ever half-applied.
- An emergency rollback script is in `.auth/rollback-00071-00072.sql`. Only use it **before** the merge, because the new code needs these objects.

## How `ehl` was set up (from the private operator notes)

| | Production |
|---|---|
| Bot account | `ehl-gg`, registered with **`ehl@tum-ai.com`** (the Google Workspace mailbox that also sends the emails) |
| Token | classic personal token, scopes `repo`, `workflow`, `delete_repo`, no expiry |
| Copy org | `european-hackathon-league`, **Free** plan; `ehl-gg` is an **admin** there; other members: you and Julian |
| Main org | `tum-ai` (owned via `admin@tum-ai.com`); code in `tum-ai/ehl` |

## Recommended test setup, mirroring that

**1. Email: an alias on the same Workspace.** In the Google Workspace admin console, add an alternate email such as **`ehl-test@tum-ai.com`** to the `ehl@` user (or create a Google Group with that address). It needs no extra license, and mail arrives in the inbox you already watch. GitHub needs its own verified address per account, so the bot can't reuse `ehl@`. A plus address (`ehl+test@tum-ai.com`) often works as a quick alternative, but the alias is cleaner.

**2. GitHub account: `ehl-test-gg`.**
- Sign up at github.com with `ehl-test@tum-ai.com` and confirm the email.
- Turn on two-factor authentication, and store the password and 2FA codes where you keep the `ehl-gg` ones (GitHub requires 2FA for accounts that push code).

**3. Org: `european-hackathon-league-test`.**
- Create it **with your own account** (Free plan), then invite `ehl-test-gg` and make it an **owner/admin**, like `ehl-gg` in production.
- Under Settings → Member privileges, set **base permission to "No permission"** and turn off "members can create repositories". Production still has "Read", the setting we discussed; the test org should start correctly.
- The Free plan is enough. The production org is also Free and holds private copies (the Zurich copies are private). That contradicts a claim in `submission-private-workaround.md` that Free orgs can't receive private forks; the real data shows they can.

**4. Token for `ehl-test-gg`.** Under Settings → Developer settings → Personal access tokens → **Tokens (classic)**: scopes **`repo`** and **`workflow`**, plus `delete_repo` if you want to clean up test copies later. Set an **expiry, e.g. 90 days**; a test token shouldn't live forever.

**5. Connect it.**
- **GitHub Actions** (`tum-ai/ehl` → Settings → Secrets and variables → Actions):
  - secret **`TEST_GH_PAT`** = the new token;
  - under the **Variables** tab, **`TEST_GITHUB_ORG`** = `european-hackathon-league-test`.
- **For the local trial run**, in `.env.test`: `GITHUB_TOKEN=<test token>`, `GITHUB_ORG=european-hackathon-league-test` and `SNAPSHOT_WORKER_ENV=test`, and turn the network guard off for that run only. Put it all back afterwards.

**6. Test material.**
- Create 2–3 **private repos under your own account** (e.g. one with Entire checkpoints, one without) and invite `ehl-test-gg` as a collaborator. Submit accepts the invite automatically.
- Use your personal account, or a second test account, as the "juror".

**7. Write it down privately.** Add the new account, alias and org to `docs/ACCOUNTS.local.md` / the `ehl-ops` repo, **not** to the public repo.

Once `ehl-test-gg`, the org and the two Actions entries exist, tell me and I'll run the trial run (step 2 of the checklist) with you against the test database.

## Steps on github.com

**1. Create the org (logged in as `mykhayloserdyuk`)**

content.text:
You're right: **a separate GitHub account isn't required.** You can run the trial with `ehl-gg` and `european-hackathon-league`. That's even the **more realistic** test, because it checks the real bot's real permissions. The checks confirm it:

- **The existing E2E tests already use production GitHub.** CI runs with `GH_PAT` (`ehl-gg`) and `GITHUB_ORG: european-hackathon-league`, and test 7.5 reads `european-hackathon-league/e2e-test-submission`.
- **Test copies can't collide with real ones.** The worker names each copy `submission-<submission id>-<repo id>`. Real event copies are named like `munich-2-…`, so a test can never write into an existing copy.
- **The quota cost is tiny.** A trial run needs a few dozen requests and a handful of writes, out of 5,000 per hour. That only matters during a live event.
- **What truly has to be separate is the database**, so test submissions never mix with real ones. That's already the case: the test Supabase is ready with 00071/00072.

What the separate account would have added, and how to cover it without it:

| Concern | Without a test account |
|---|---|
| Test copies show up in the production org | They're clearly named `submission-<id>-…`; delete them after the test (`ehl-gg` has `delete_repo`) |
| Shared request allowance | Don't test during an event, which is already the plan |
| Accidental real jury invites | Leave "invite jury to forks" off in the test challenge, or assign only your own account as juror |

## Trial run setup with `ehl-gg`

**Local** (`.env.test`, for that run only):
```
SNAPSHOT_WORKER_ENV=test
GITHUB_TOKEN=<ehl-gg token, same as GH_PAT>
GITHUB_ORG=european-hackathon-league
```
Turn the network guard off for that run and put everything back afterwards. In test mode the worker requires token and org to be **set explicitly**; it doesn't care which account they belong to.

**Optional post-merge test workflow:** set `TEST_GH_PAT` to the same `ehl-gg` token and `TEST_GITHUB_ORG` to `european-hackathon-league`. Or skip it: the local trial run already covers the important parts.

**`ehl-test-gg`:** you can leave it unused or delete it. If you ever want strict separation (e.g. load tests during the season), it's ready. The org `european-hackathon-league-test` doesn't need to be created.

Should we start the trial run that way? You'd need to give me 2–3 private test repos under your account with `ehl-gg` invited (one with Entire checkpoints, one without).

content.text:
Yes, I have a plan. It's below with every step, what it measures, and the formula for the capacity numbers. Before I start, there's one important adjustment to your juror request, plus three things I need your OK for.

## One adjustment: your own account can't serve as the test juror

Your account `mykhayloserdyuk` is an **owner of `european-hackathon-league`**, so you can already read every repo in it. Inviting you to a copy would never create a real invitation, and wouldn't show what a normal juror experiences or what it costs.

**`ehl-test-gg` is the ideal test juror**: not an org member, and you control it, so you can accept the invite and open the code like a real juror. That puts the new account to good use. I can additionally invite your account to show it's a no-op, but the measurement should use `ehl-test-gg`.

## The plan

**Setup (test database only, plus GitHub under your account)**
1. **4 private test repos under `mykhayloserdyuk`**: `ehl-rehearsal-1` … `-4`, each with a few commits, and **`ehl-gg` invited** as a collaborator.
   - `-1` to `-3`: normal private repos, which give the base cost per team.
   - `-4`: has Entire checkpoints. I'd create them in the exact format the unit tests use, unless you have a real repo with Entire that I should copy instead.
2. **In the test database**, using the existing test helpers:
   - one chapter in `submissions_open` and two challenges with a repo field: one private-only with **"invite jury to forks" on**, one with Entire required;
   - 4 teams with checked-in, registered members;
   - juror `ehl-test-gg` with that GitHub username.
   - **AI review stays off** (it would cost OpenRouter money); I measure the review's single archive download separately, with no AI.
3. **Local app against the test database**, using the real `ehl-gg` token and the `european-hackathon-league` org, with the network guard off for this run.

**Run (each step with its quota measurement)**

For every step I read the bot's counter (`GET /rate_limit`, which itself costs nothing) **before and after**, and the worker's own write counter in the database. That gives exact reads and writes per step.

| Step | What I check | What I measure |
|---|---|---|
| A. Submit `-1` **without** the bot invited | refused with "cannot read" | requests of a refused attempt |
| B. Submit all 4 through the real form | saved; recorded commit = repo's current commit | **requests per Submit** (normal vs Entire) |
| C. Entire repo **without** checkpoints | refused | requests of a refused Entire check |
| D. Run the worker | private copies `submission-<id>-…` exist; `ehl-final/1` = recorded commit | **requests and writes per copy**; whether the git transfer costs REST requests (it shouldn't) |
| E. Push to `-2`, don't update | recorded commit unchanged | 0 |
| F. "Update Submission" on `-2` | new commit recorded and copied | **cost of a resubmit** |
| G. Stop the worker mid-copy, restart | continues cleanly, no duplicates | — |
| H. Deadline → lock | chapter "pitching", Update refused, GitHub not called | **0 requests** at the deadline |
| I. Worker after lock | `ehl-test-gg` invited to each private copy | **writes per juror per repo** |
| J. As `ehl-test-gg`: accept invites, open jury links | the recorded commit opens | — |
| K. Review archive for one copy | one zip download, parsed | **requests per review** |

**Result: the capacity calculation from measured numbers**
- Per team: `Submit + copy + jurors × invite (+ review)`, split into reads and writes.
- Against the limits: the bot's **5,000 requests per hour**, the worker's **400 writes per hour**, and GitHub's ~80 writes per minute.
- A table: **how many teams in the hour after the deadline, for 0–5 jurors per challenge and 0 %/33 %/67 %/100 % private repos**, with and without the "teams invite jurors themselves" option from `submission-private-workaround.md`.

**Cleanup:** delete the test copies in the org (`submission-*`) and the 4 test repos, remove the test data, put `.env.test` back.

Time: about 1.5–2 hours, mostly waiting on GitHub forks and checks. It must not run during a live event; it doesn't, since no match is open.

## I need your OK for these outside actions

1. **Create the 4 private repos under your account** (`mykhayloserdyuk/ehl-rehearsal-1…4`) and invite `ehl-gg`. I'd do that with your logged-in `gh`.
2. **Temporary private copies in `european-hackathon-league`**, named `submission-<id>-…`, deleted at the end.
3. **Invites to `ehl-test-gg`** for those copies. For step J I need you to accept them while logged in as `ehl-test-gg`, or to give me a token for that account; a browser login is enough.

Plus one question: **should the Entire repo use synthetic checkpoints** (the format from the unit tests), **or do you have a real repo with Entire** that I should copy?

create or replace function try_acquire_cron_lock(
  lock_key text,
  ttl_seconds integer
)
returns boolean
language plpgsql
as $$
declare
  acquired boolean;
begin
  insert into app_settings (key, value, expires_at, updated_at)
  values (lock_key, 'locked', now() + make_interval(secs => ttl_seconds), now())
  on conflict (key) do update
    set value = 'locked',
        expires_at = now() + make_interval(secs => ttl_seconds),
        updated_at = now()
    -- Only steal the lock if the current holder's lease has expired.
    where app_settings.expires_at is null
       or app_settings.expires_at < now()
  returning true into acquired;

  return coalesce(acquired, false);
end;
$$;
create or replace function release_cron_lock(lock_key text)
returns void
language sql
as $$
  update app_settings set expires_at = null where key = lock_key;
$$;

content.text:
**Every box is ticked except J, which needs you as `ehl-test-gg`.** The flow works end to end with the real bot and real private repos. The crash test turned up one notable finding.

## Results

| Step | Check | Result |
|---|---|---|
| A | Private repo, bot not invited → Submit | ✅ refused: "We cannot read this repository…" |
| B | 5 Submits (bot invite pending, accepted, Entire with 40 checkpoints) | ✅ saved; recorded commit = repo head; Submit accepts the bot invite itself |
| C | Entire challenge, repo without checkpoints | ✅ refused with the Entire message |
| D | Worker copies | ✅ 5 **private** copies; `ehl-final/1` = recorded commit; all **40 checkpoints** copied exactly |
| E | Push without Update | ✅ recorded and copied version unchanged |
| F | "Update Submission" | ✅ new commit recorded, copy updated **without a new fork**; old version kept as `ehl-final/1` |
| G | Worker killed hard mid-copy | ✅ resumed without a duplicate fork and finished correctly. ⚠️ **Finding:** after a crash the lock stays held for **up to 30 minutes**; restarts do nothing until then |
| H | Deadline | ✅ 0 GitHub requests; later Update refused **before** any GitHub call |
| I | Jury invites after the deadline | ✅ `ehl-test-gg` invited to all 5 copies, **read-only** |
| K | Review code download | ✅ 1 API request (the download itself doesn't count) |
| **J** | **Juror accepts the invites and opens the code** | ⏳ **your turn** (see below) |

## Measured costs per team (exact, logged per request)

| Action | Reads | Writes |
|---|---|---|
| Submit (bot invite already accepted) | 2 | 0 |
| Submit with bot invite still pending | 4 | 1 |
| Submit, Entire challenge (40 checkpoints, check stops at first prompt) | 5 | 0 |
| Each further "Update Submission" | 2–5 | 0 |
| First copy (fork) | 4 | 1 |
| Re-copy after an Update | 3 | 0 |
| Deadline lock | 0 | 0 |
| After the deadline, per team | 1 | **1 per juror** |
| AI review download | 1 | 0 |
| Git transfer of the code | 0 | 0 |

**So per team: about 10–15 requests in total, 2 writes, plus 1 write per juror.**

## What limits capacity

- **The 5,000 requests per hour are not the bottleneck.** Even 150 teams with 5 jurors and an Update each use about 3,000–4,000.
- **The bottleneck is jury invites after the deadline.** The worker sends at most **20 writes per minute** (measured: 3 seconds per invite) and **400 per hour**.

Time until **the last juror has access** (all repos private, invites on; teams of a challenge × that challenge's jurors):

| Teams | 1 juror | 3 jurors | 5 jurors |
|---|---|---|---|
| 40 | 2 min | 6 min | 10 min |
| 60 | 3 min | 9 min | 15 min |
| 80 | 4 min | 12 min | **20 min** (exactly 400) |
| 100 | 5 min | 15 min | **~65 min** (500 > 400: waits for the next hour) |
| 150 | 8 min | **~63 min** | **~78 min** |

Two adjustments to the table:
- **Copies created in the hour before the deadline also count toward the 400**, at 1 write each. Many late submitters push these times up.
- With the **workaround (teams invite jurors themselves, invites off)**, the bot sends **0 writes** after the deadline, so jury access no longer depends on the bot. Copies run at about 5 seconds each, so 80 last-minute submissions are copied in about 7 minutes.

## Your step J (about 5 minutes)

1. Log in to GitHub as **`ehl-test-gg`**.
2. Accept the 5 invitations at github.com/notifications, or at each repo's `/invitations` page.

content.text:
Thanks for checking J. With that, **every box of the trial run is ticked.** Answers to your two questions first, then the cleanup.

## 1. Inviting jurors before vs. after the deadline

There are no "tokens" being used up here. The point is **how many write operations the bot sends to GitHub within a short time**:

- Each jury invite is **one write per juror per repo**: "give `ehl-test-gg` read access to this copy". GitHub limits writes much more strictly than reads. Our worker therefore sends **at most one write every 3 seconds (20 per minute)** and **at most 400 per hour**.
- **The number of invites is the same either way.** 80 teams × 5 jurors = 400 invites, whether they're sent at 10:00 or at 15:00.
- **What differs is when they pile up.** The worker currently sends all invites **only after the deadline**, so all 400 queue up exactly when judging starts, and the last jurors wait until the queue is through. Sent earlier, the same 400 would trickle out over the event and be done by the deadline.

So "after the deadline" isn't more expensive. It's a traffic jam at the worst moment.

## 2. How to read the table

Each cell is **the time until the last juror can open the last repo**, **for all teams together**, not per team.

**Calculation:**
1. **Number of invites = teams × jurors.** Each juror is invited to every copy in their challenge.
2. **The worker sends 20 invites per minute** (measured: one every 3 seconds).
3. **Minutes = invites ÷ 20.**

| Example | Invites | Calculation | Result |
|---|---|---|---|
| 80 teams, 1 juror | 80 | 80 ÷ 20 | **4 min** |
| 80 teams, 5 jurors | 400 | 400 ÷ 20 | **20 min** |
| 100 teams, 5 jurors | 500 | first 400 in 20 min; then the **400/hour cap** forces a wait until minute 60; the remaining 100 take 5 more min | **~65 min** |

**Per team** that's simply **3 seconds per juror**: 5 jurors means one team's copy is fully shared after 15 seconds. The total is long only because the teams are processed one after another.

Two notes:
- If copies were also created in the hour before the deadline, they use part of the 400 too (1 write per copy).
- With the workaround (teams invite jurors themselves), the bot sends **0** invites, so the table no longer applies.

## 3. Cleanup

Now removing everything the trial run created. Before deleting, I'll check that each copy really is one of the five test copies (name `submission-…` and source repo `ehl-rehearsal-…`), so nothing real can be hit.

content.text:
Fixed, tested, and committed locally (not pushed yet). After a crash, the next worker now takes over within **about 2–3 minutes instead of 30**.

**What changed** (commit `145dbaf`, on top of the 7 existing commits):
- **The worker lock is a 90-second lock that a running worker renews every 30 seconds.** If the worker dies, it stops renewing and the lock expires after at most 90 seconds.
- **The dispatch lock drops from 5 minutes to 90 seconds**, so the cron can start a replacement quickly.
- Safety is unchanged: per-job locks and revision checks keep two briefly overlapping workers from ever copying the same job twice.

**Verified:**

| Check | Result |
|---|---|
| Real crash against the test database | killed at 10:57:03, **next run took over at 10:58:28 (85 s)**; the lock was renewed while the worker was alive |
| 6 new unit tests (written first, failed on the old code) | ✅ |
| All unit tests | ✅ 1,423 of 1,423 |
| Build, typecheck | ✅ |
| E2E lifecycle | ✅ 76 of 76 |
| Docs | `docs/SETUP.md` now states the ~2-minute recovery |

Worst case after a crash is now: up to 90 seconds until the lock expires, the next cron minute, and about 30–60 seconds for GitHub Actions to start a fresh worker.

**One thing this does not solve:** even without any crash, the jury invites themselves take time after the deadline: **80 teams × 5 jurors ≈ 20 minutes** (one invite every 3 seconds). If jurors need access the moment pitching starts, that delay remains. The workaround from `submission-private-workaround.md` (invites off; teams invite jurors themselves) removes it entirely.

**Waiting for your OK** before anything public:
1. **Push** commit `145dbaf` to `fix/submission-snapshot-queue`. PR #122 updates automatically, and CI runs again.
2. **Change one sentence in the PR description.** Replace

   > A worker killed mid-run keeps its 30-minute lock, so copies resume only after it expires; nothing is lost or duplicated.

   with

   > A worker killed mid-run is replaced within about two minutes: its lock is a 90-second lease renewed while it runs (measured: the next run took over 85 seconds after the kill), and nothing is lost or duplicated.

Should I push and update the description?
